Warsaw,[b] officially the Capital City of Warsaw,[11][c] is the capital and most populous city of Poland.[12][13] The metropolis stands on the river Vistula in east-central Poland. Its population is officially estimated at 1.87 million residents within a greater metropolitan area of around 3.5 million residents, which makes Warsaw the 7th most populous city in the European Union.[6] The city area measures 517 square kilometres (200 square miles) and comprises 18 districts, while the metropolitan area covers 6,100 square kilometres (2,355 square miles).[14] Warsaw is classified as an alpha global city,[15] a major political, economic and cultural hub, and the country's seat of government. It is also the capital of the Masovian Voivodeship.

Warsaw traces its origins to a small fishing town which became the seat of the Duchy of Masovia in 1413. The city rose to prominence after 1596, when Sigismund III decided to move the Polish capital and his royal court from Kraków. Warsaw surpassed Gdańsk as Poland's most populous city by the 18th century. It served as the capital of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth until 1795, and subsequently as the seat of Napoleon's Duchy of Warsaw. The 19th century and its Industrial Revolution brought a demographic boom, which made it one of the largest and most densely populated cities in Europe. Known then for its elegant architecture and boulevards, Warsaw was bombed and besieged at the start of World War II in 1939.[16][17][18] Much of the historic city was destroyed and its diverse population decimated by the Ghetto Uprising in 1943, the general Warsaw Uprising in 1944, and systematic razing.

Warsaw is served by three international airports, the busiest being Warsaw Chopin Airport. Major public transport services operating in the city include the Warsaw Metro, buses, commuter rail service and an extensive tram network. The city is a significant economic centre for the region, with the Warsaw Stock Exchange being the largest in Central and Eastern Europe.[19][20] It is the base for Frontex, the EU agency for external border security; also ODIHR, one of the principal institutions of the OSCE and an ESA headquarters. Warsaw has one of Europe's largest concentrations of skyscrapers, and the Varso Tower is the tallest building in the European Union.

The city's primary educational and cultural institutions include the University of Warsaw, the Warsaw University of Technology, the SGH Warsaw School of Economics, the Chopin University of Music, the Polish Academy of Sciences, the National Philharmonic Orchestra, the National Museum, and the Warsaw Grand Theatre, which is among the largest in Europe.[21] The reconstructed Old Town, which represents a variety of European architectural styles, was listed as a World Heritage Site by UNESCO in 1980.[22] Other landmarks include the Royal Castle, Sigismund's Column, the Wilanów Palace, the Palace on the Isle, St. John's Archcathedral, Main Market Square, and numerous churches and mansions along the Royal Route. Warsaw is a green capital, with around a quarter of the city's area occupied by parks.[23][24] In sports, the city is home to Legia and Polonia sports clubs and hosts the annual Warsaw Marathon.

Toponymy and names
For the name of Warsaw in various languages, see wikt:Warsaw.

Warsaw's name in the Polish language is Warszawa. Other previous spellings of the name may have included: Warszewa, Warszowa, Worszewa or Werszewa.[25][26] The exact origin and meaning of the name is uncertain and has not been fully determined.[27][28] Originally, Warszawa was the name of a small fishing settlement on the banks of the Vistula river. One hypothesis states that Warszawa means "belonging to Warsz", Warsz being a shortened form of the masculine Old Polish name Warcisław, which etymologically is linked with Wrocław.[29] However the ending -awa is unusual for a large city; the names of Polish cities derived from personal names usually end in -ów/owo/ew/ewo (e.g. Piotrków, Adamów).

Folk etymology attributes the city name to Wars and Sawa. There are several versions of the legend with their appearance. According to one version, Sawa was a mermaid living in the Vistula with whom fisherman Wars fell in love.[30][31] The official city name in full is miasto stołeczne Warszawa ("The Capital City of Warsaw").[32]

A native or resident of Warsaw is known as a Varsovian – in Polish warszawiak,[d] warszawianin[e] (male); warszawianka (female); warszawiacy, and warszawianie (plural).

History
Main article: History of Warsaw
For a chronological guide, see Timeline of Warsaw.
1300–1800

The first fortified settlements on the site of today's Warsaw were located in Bródno (9th/10th century) and Jazdów (12th/13th century).[33] After Jazdów was raided by nearby clans and dukes, a new fortified settlement was established on the site of a small fishing village called "Warszowa". The Prince of Płock, Bolesław II of Masovia, established the modern-day city in about 1300 and the first historical document attesting to the existence of a castellany dates to 1313.[34] With the completion of St John's Cathedral in 1390, Warsaw became one of the seats of the Dukes of Masovia and was officially made capital of the Masovian Duchy in 1413.[33] The economy then predominantly rested on craftsmanship or trade, and the town housed approximately 4,500 people at the time.

An engraving from Civitates orbis terrarum of 16th-century Warsaw showing the Sigismund Augustus Bridge and St. Mary's Church to the right, and St. John's Archcathedral visible at the centre.

During the 15th century, the population migrated and spread beyond the northern city wall into a newly formed self-governing precinct called New Town. The existing older settlement became eventually known as the Old Town. Both possessed their own town charter and independent councils. The aim of establishing a separate district was to accommodate new incomers or "undesirables" who were not permitted to settle in Old Town, particularly Jews.[35] Social and financial disparities between the classes in the two precincts led to a minor revolt in 1525.[34] Following the sudden death of Janusz III and the extinction of the local ducal line, Masovia was incorporated into the Kingdom of Poland in 1526.[33] Bona Sforza, wife of Sigismund I of Poland, was widely accused of poisoning the duke to uphold Polish rule over Warsaw.[36][37]

In 1529, Warsaw for the first time became the seat of a General Sejm and held that privilege permanently from 1569.[33] The city's rising importance encouraged the construction of a new set of defenses, including the landmark Barbican. Renowned Italian architects were brought to Warsaw to reshape the Royal Castle, the streets and the marketplace, resulting in the Old Town's early Italianate appearance. In 1573, the city gave its name to the Warsaw Confederation which formally established religious freedom in the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth. Due to its central location between the capitals of the Commonwealth's two component parts, Poland and Lithuania, which were Kraków and Vilnius respectively, Warsaw became the capital of the Commonwealth and the Polish Crown when Sigismund III Vasa transferred his royal court in 1596.[33] In the subsequent years the town significantly expanded to the south and westwards. Several private independent districts (jurydyka) were the property of aristocrats and the gentry, which they ruled by their own laws. Between 1655 and 1658 the city was besieged and pillaged by the Swedish, Brandenburgian and Transylvanian forces.[33][38] The conduct of the Great Northern War (1700–1721) also forced Warsaw to pay heavy tributes to the invading armies.[39]

The reign of Augustus II, Augustus III and Stanisław August Poniatowski was a time of great development for Warsaw, which turned into an early-capitalist city. The Saxon monarchs employed many German architects, sculptors and engineers, who added elements to the city in a style parallel with Dresden, chiefly the Saxon Axis, while Poniatowski boosted the native Polish architectural and artisanal scene. The year 1727 marked the opening of the Saxon Garden in Warsaw, the first publicly accessible park.[40] The Załuski Library, the first Polish public library and the largest at the time, was founded in 1747.[41] Stanisław II Augustus, who remodelled the interior of the Royal Castle, also made Warsaw a centre of culture and the arts.[42][43] He extended the Royal Baths Park and ordered the construction or refurbishment of numerous palaces, mansions and richly decorated tenements. This earned Warsaw the nickname Paris of the North.[44] Stanisław August Poniatowski created the first state theater in Warsaw, invested in the Royal Baths Park and created the Stanislavian Axis (Polish: Oś Stanisławowska), a large infrastructural undertaking.

Warsaw New Town in 1778. Painted by Bernardo Bellotto.

Warsaw remained the capital of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth until 1795 when it was annexed by the Kingdom of Prussia in the third and final partition of Poland;[45] it subsequently became the capital of the province of South Prussia. During this time, Louis XVIII of France spent his exile in Warsaw under the pseudonym Comte de Lille.[46]

1800–1939

Warsaw was made the capital of a newly created French client state, known as the Duchy of Warsaw, after a portion of Poland's territory was liberated from Prussia, Russia and Austria by Napoleon in 1806.[33] Following Napoleon's defeat and exile, the 1815 Congress of Vienna assigned Warsaw to Congress Poland, a constitutional monarchy within the easternmost sector (or partition) under a personal union with Imperial Russia.[33] The Royal University of Warsaw was established in 1816.

With the violation of the Polish constitution, the 1830 November Uprising broke out against foreign influence. The Polish-Russian war of 1831 ended in the uprising's defeat and in the curtailment of Congress Poland's autonomy.[33] On 27 February 1861, a Warsaw crowd protesting against Russian control over Congress Poland was fired upon by Russian troops.[47][48] Five people were killed. The Underground Polish National Government resided in Warsaw during the January Uprising in 1863–64.[48]

Warsaw flourished throughout the 19th century under Mayor Sokrates Starynkiewicz (1875–92), who was appointed by Alexander III. Under Starynkiewicz Warsaw saw its first water and sewer systems designed and built by the English engineer William Lindley and his son, William Heerlein Lindley, as well as the expansion and modernisation of trams, street lighting, and gas infrastructure.[33] Between 1850 and 1882, the population grew by 134% to 383,000 as a result of rapid urbanisation and industrialisation. Many migrated from surrounding rural Masovian towns and villages to the city for employment opportunities. The western borough of Wola was transformed from an agricultural periphery occupied mostly by small farms and windmills (mills being the namesake of Wola's central neighbourhood Młynów) to an industrial and manufacturing centre.[49] Metallurgical, textile and glassware factories were commonplace, with chimneys dominating the westernmost skyline.[50]

Marszałkowska Street, before 1920
National Philharmonic, before 1906

Like London, Warsaw's population was subjected to income segmentation. Gentrification of inner suburbs forced poorer residents to move across the river into Praga or Powiśle and Solec districts, similar to the East End of London and London Docklands.[51] Poorer religious and ethnic minorities, such as the Jews, settled in the crowded parts of northern Warsaw, in Muranów.[52] The Imperial Census of 1897 recorded 626,000 people living in Warsaw, making it the third-largest city of the Empire after St. Petersburg and Moscow as well as the largest city in the region.[53] Grand architectural complexes and structures were also erected in the city centre, including the Warsaw Philharmonic, the Church of the Holiest Saviour and tenements along Marszałkowska Street.

During World War I, Warsaw was occupied by Germany from 4 August 1915 until November 1918. The Armistice of 11 November 1918 concluded that defeated Germany is to withdraw from all foreign areas, which included Warsaw.[54] Germany did so, and underground leader Józef Piłsudski returned to Warsaw on the same day which marked the beginning of the Second Polish Republic, the first truly sovereign Polish state after 1795. In the course of the Polish–Soviet War (1919–1921), the 1920 Battle of Warsaw was fought on the eastern outskirts of the city. Poland successfully defended the capital, stopped the brunt of the Bolshevik Red Army and temporarily halted the "export of the communist revolution" to other parts of Europe.[55]

The interwar period (1918–1939) was a time of major development in the city's infrastructure. New modernist housing estates were built in Mokotów to de-clutter the densely populated inner suburbs. In 1921, Warsaw's total area was estimated at only 124.7 km2 (48.1 sq mi) with 1 million inhabitants–over 8,000 people/km2 made Warsaw more densely populated than contemporary London.[56] The Średnicowy Bridge was constructed for railway (1921–1931), connecting both parts of the city across the Vistula. Warszawa Główna railway station (1932–1939) was not completed due to the outbreak of the Second World War.

Stefan Starzyński was the Mayor of Warsaw between 1934 and 1939.

World War II
The Warsaw Uprising took place in 1944. The Polish Home Army attempted to liberate Warsaw from the Germans before the arrival of the Red Army.[57]

After the German invasion of Poland on 1 September 1939 started World War II, Warsaw was defended until 27 September. Central Poland, including Warsaw, came under the rule of the General Government, a German Nazi colonial administration. All higher education institutions were immediately closed and Warsaw's entire Jewish population – several hundred thousand, some 30% of the city – were herded into the Warsaw Ghetto.[58] In July 1942, the Jews of the Warsaw Ghetto began to be deported en masse to the Aktion Reinhard extermination camps, particularly Treblinka.[58] The city would become the centre of urban resistance to Nazi rule in occupied Europe.[59] When the order came to annihilate the ghetto as part of Hitler's "Final Solution" on 19 April 1943, Jewish fighters launched the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising.[60] Despite being heavily outgunned and outnumbered, the ghetto held out for almost a month.[60] When the fighting ended, almost all survivors were massacred, with only a few managing to escape or hide.[60][61]

By July 1944, the Red Army was deep into Polish territory and pursuing the Nazis toward Warsaw.[62] The Polish government-in-exile in London gave orders to the underground Home Army (AK) to try to seize control of Warsaw before the Red Army arrived. Thus, on 1 August 1944, as the Red Army was nearing the city, the Warsaw Uprising began.[62] The armed struggle, planned to last 48 hours, was partially successful, however, it went on for 63 days. Eventually, the Home Army fighters and civilians assisting them were forced to capitulate.[62] They were transported to PoW camps in Germany, while the entire civilian population was expelled.[62] Polish civilian deaths are estimated at between 150,000 and 200,000.[63]

Hitler, ignoring the agreed terms of the capitulation, ordered the entire city to be razed to the ground and the library and museum collections taken to Germany or burned.[62] Monuments and government buildings were blown up by special German troops known as Verbrennungs- und Vernichtungskommando ("Burning and Destruction Detachments").[62] About 85% of the city was destroyed, including the historic Old Town and the Royal Castle.[64]

On 17 January 1945 – after the beginning of the Vistula–Oder Offensive of the Red Army – Soviet troops and Polish troops of the First Polish Army entered the ruins of Warsaw, and liberated Warsaw's suburbs from German occupation.[65] The city was swiftly freed by the Soviet Army, which rapidly advanced towards Łódź, as German forces regrouped at a more westward position.

1945–1989

**Theatre Square** ([Polish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language "Polish language"): _plac Teatralny_) is a major square in the [Śródmieście](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C5%9Ar%C3%B3dmie%C5%9Bcie,_Warsaw "Śródmieście, Warsaw") district of [Warsaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warsaw "Warsaw"), [Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poland "Poland"). It spans from the [Great Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Theatre,_Warsaw "Great Theatre, Warsaw") building to Senatorska Street.

The origins of the square date back to the beginning of the 19th century, when a small square was established in 1818. From 1825 to 1832, the Great Theatre building was constructed. When the city administration was relocated to the [Jabłonowski Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jab%C5%82onowski_Palace "Jabłonowski Palace"), the square became a centre of city life. Various patriotic demonstrations took place there, including at the time of the failed [January Uprising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/January_Uprising "January Uprising") and the [Revolution of 1905](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revolution_of_1905 "Revolution of 1905").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre_Square_(Warsaw)#cite_note-Srodmiescie-1)

In [September 1939](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invasion_of_Poland "Invasion of Poland"), the civilian defense of the city was located in the city hall. During the [Warsaw Uprising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warsaw_Uprising "Warsaw Uprising") of 1944, the square witnessed [heavy fighting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_war_crimes_at_Theatre_Square_in_Warsaw "Nazi war crimes at Theatre Square in Warsaw") between the Nazi German soldiers and the [Home Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armia_Krajowa "Armia Krajowa") partisans. Most of the surrounding buildings were heavily damaged or completely destroyed.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatre_Square_(Warsaw)#cite_note-Srodmiescie-1) After the war, several buildings were restored, excluding the pre-war city hall with its notable clock tower. It was rebuilt according to the original architectural plans only in the late 1990s.

## Landmarks

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Theatre_Square_(Warsaw)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Landmarks")]

Landmarks on the square include:

*   The [Great Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Theatre,_Warsaw "Great Theatre, Warsaw") (reconstructed 1951–65)
*   The [Jabłonowski Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jab%C5%82onowski_Palace "Jabłonowski Palace") (reconstructed 1995–97)
*   The [Blank Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blank_Palace "Blank Palace") (named after Piotr Blank, banker to the last king of the [Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish%E2%80%93Lithuanian_Commonwealth "Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth"), [Stanisław II Augustus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanis%C5%82aw_II_Augustus "Stanisław II Augustus"))
*   Saints Albert and Andrew's Church (_Kościół św. Brata Alberta i św. Andrzeja Apostoła_ – a church for the Warsaw creative communities), reconstructed in 1999)
*   Petyskus House (_Kamienica Petyskusa_), restored in 1950
*   The [Warsaw Meridian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warsaw_meridian "Warsaw meridian") (a marker for the [meridian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meridian_(geography) "Meridian (geography)"), set up in 1880 – since superseded by [Greenwich Mean Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenwich_Mean_Time "Greenwich Mean Time"))

**Polish** ([endonym](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endonym_and_exonym "Endonym and exonym"): _język polski_, [[ˈjɛ̃zɘ̟k ˈpɔlskʲi]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Polish "Help:IPA/Polish")[](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/d/d9/Pl-j%C4%99zyk_polski.ogg/Pl-j%C4%99zyk_polski.ogg.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pl-j%C4%99zyk_polski.ogg "File:Pl-język polski.ogg"), _polszczyzna_[[pɔlˈʂt͡ʂɘ̟zna]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Polish "Help:IPA/Polish")[](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/4/47/Pl-polszczyzna.ogg/Pl-polszczyzna.ogg.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pl-polszczyzna.ogg "File:Pl-polszczyzna.ogg") or simply _polski_, [[ˈpɔlskʲi]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Polish "Help:IPA/Polish")[](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/d/d8/Pl-polski.ogg/Pl-polski.ogg.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pl-polski.ogg "File:Pl-polski.ogg")) is a [West Slavic language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Slavic_languages "West Slavic languages") of the [Lechitic subgroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lechitic_languages "Lechitic languages"), within the [Indo-European language family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indo-European_languages "Indo-European languages"), and is written in the [Latin script](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_script "Latin script").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-15) It is primarily spoken in [Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poland "Poland") and serves as the [official language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Official_language "Official language") of the country, as well as the language of the [Polish diaspora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_diaspora "Polish diaspora") around the world. In 2024, there were over 39.7 million Polish native speakers.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-ethnologue-16) It ranks as the sixth-most-spoken among [languages of the European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Languages_of_the_European_Union "Languages of the European Union").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-17) Polish is subdivided into regional [dialects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dialects_of_Polish "Dialects of Polish"). It maintains strict [T–V distinction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T%E2%80%93V_distinction "T–V distinction"), obligatory [honorifics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honorifics_(linguistics) "Honorifics (linguistics)"), and other formalities when addressing individuals.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-18)

The traditional 32-letter [Polish alphabet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_alphabet "Polish alphabet") has nine additions (_ą_, _ć_, _ę_, _ł_, _ń_, _ó_, _ś_, _ź_, _ż_) to the letters of the basic 26-letter [Latin alphabet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_alphabet "Latin alphabet"), while removing three (x, q, v). Those three letters are at times included in an extended 35-letter alphabet.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-sjp.pwn.pl-19) The traditional set comprises 23 [consonants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consonants "Consonants") and nine written [vowels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vowels "Vowels"), including two [nasal vowels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasal_vowels "Nasal vowels") (_ę_, _ą_) denoted by a reversed [diacritic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diacritic "Diacritic") hook called an _[ogonek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ogonek "Ogonek")_.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-20) Polish is a [synthetic and fusional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fusional_language "Fusional language") language which has seven [grammatical cases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammatical_case "Grammatical case").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-21) It has fixed [penultimate stress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stress_(linguistics) "Stress (linguistics)") and an abundance of [palatal consonants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palatal_consonants "Palatal consonants").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-22) Contemporary Polish developed in the 1700s as the successor to the medieval [Old Polish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Polish "Old Polish") (10th–16th centuries) and [Middle Polish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Polish "Middle Polish") (16th–18th centuries).[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-23)

Among the major languages, it is most closely related to [Slovak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovak_language "Slovak language")[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-24) and [Czech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Czech_language "Czech language")[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-Swan-2002-25) but differs in terms of pronunciation and general grammar. In addition, Polish was profoundly influenced by [Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin "Latin") and other [Romance languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romance_languages "Romance languages") like [Italian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_language "Italian language") and [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language") as well as [Germanic languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germanic_languages "Germanic languages") (most notably [German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_language "German language")), which contributed a large number of loanwords and grammatical structures.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-26)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-27)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-28) Extensive usage of [nonstandard dialects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonstandard_dialect "Nonstandard dialect") has also shaped the [standard language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_language "Standard language"); many [colloquialisms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colloquialism "Colloquialism") and expressions were directly borrowed from German or [Yiddish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yiddish "Yiddish") and subsequently adopted into the [vernacular](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vernacular "Vernacular") of Polish in everyday use.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-29)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-30)

Historically, Polish was a _[lingua franca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lingua\_franca "Lingua franca")_,[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-31)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-32) important both diplomatically and academically in [Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Europe "Central Europe") and part of [Eastern Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Europe "Eastern Europe"). In addition to being the official language of Poland, Polish is also spoken as a [second language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_language "Second language") in eastern [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany"), northern [Czech Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Czech_Republic "Czech Republic") and [Slovakia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia "Slovakia"), western parts of [Belarus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belarus "Belarus") and [Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukraine "Ukraine") as well as in southeast [Lithuania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithuania "Lithuania") and [Latvia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latvia "Latvia"). Because of the emigration from Poland during different time periods, most notably after [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), millions of Polish speakers can also be found in countries such as [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada"), [Argentina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentina "Argentina"), [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil "Brazil"), [Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel "Israel"), [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia "Australia"), the [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom") and the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Polish_language&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

Main article: [History of Polish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Polish "History of Polish")

See also: [Old Polish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Polish "Old Polish") and [Middle Polish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Polish "Middle Polish")

Polish began to emerge as a distinct language around the 10th century, the process largely triggered by the establishment and development of the Polish state. At the time, it was a collection of dialect groups with some mutual features, but much regional variation was present.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-Dejna-33):235[Mieszko I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mieszko_I_of_Poland "Mieszko I of Poland"), ruler of the Polans tribe from the [Greater Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Poland "Greater Poland") region, united a few culturally and linguistically related tribes from the basins of the [Vistula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vistula "Vistula") and [Oder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oder "Oder") before eventually accepting baptism in 966. With the arrival of [Western Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Christianity "Western Christianity"), Poland also adopted the [Latin alphabet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_alphabet "Latin alphabet"), which made it possible to write down Polish, which until then had existed only as a [spoken language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spoken_language "Spoken language").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-34) The closest relatives of Polish are the [Elbe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elbe_Slavs "Elbe Slavs") and [Baltic Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pomeranians_(tribe) "Pomeranians (tribe)") Lechitic dialects ([Polabian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polabian_language "Polabian language") and [Pomeranian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pomeranian_language "Pomeranian language") varieties). All of them, except [Kashubian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kashubian_language "Kashubian language"), are extinct.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-Kolaczyk-35) The precursor to modern Polish is the [Old Polish language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Polish_language "Old Polish language"). Ultimately, Polish descends from the unattested [Proto-Slavic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Slavic "Proto-Slavic") language.

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9c/Book_of_Henryk%C3%B3w.PNG/250px-Book_of_Henryk%C3%B3w.PNG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Book_of_Henryk%C3%B3w.PNG)

The [Book of Henryków](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book_of_Henryk%C3%B3w "Book of Henryków") is the earliest document to include a sentence written entirely in what can be interpreted as [Old Polish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Polish_language "Old Polish language") – _Day, ut ia pobrusa, a ti poziwai_, meaning "let me grind, and you have a rest" highlighted in red.

The [Book of Henryków](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book_of_Henryk%C3%B3w "Book of Henryków") (Polish: _Księga henrykowska_, [Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_language "Latin language"): _Liber fundationis claustri Sanctae Mariae Virginis in Heinrichau_), contains the earliest known sentence written in the Polish language: _Day, ut ia pobrusa, a ti poziwai_ (in modern orthography: _Daj, uć ja pobrusza, a ti pocziwaj_; the corresponding sentence in modern Polish: _Daj, niech ja pomielę, a ty odpoczywaj_ or _Pozwól, że ja będę mełł, a ty odpocznij_; and in English: _Come, let me grind, and you take a rest_), written around 1280. The book is exhibited in the Archdiocesal Museum in Wrocław, in 2015 was added to [UNESCO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNESCO "UNESCO")'s "[Memory of the World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memory_of_the_World_Programme "Memory of the World Programme")" list.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-36)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-37)

The medieval recorder of this phrase, the Cistercian monk Peter of the Henryków monastery, noted that "Hoc est in polonico" ("This is in Polish").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-38)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-39)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-40)

The earliest treatise on Polish orthography was written by [Jakub Parkosz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jakub_Parkosz?action=edit&redlink=1 "Jakub Parkosz (page does not exist)")[[pl](https://pl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jakub%20Parkoszowic "pl:Jakub Parkoszowic")] around 1470.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-41) The first [printed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_printing_in_Poland "History of printing in Poland") book in Polish appeared in either 1508[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-42) or 1513,[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-Comrie-43) while the [oldest Polish newspaper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merkuriusz_Polski_Ordynaryjny "Merkuriusz Polski Ordynaryjny") was established in 1661.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-44) Starting in the 1520s, large numbers of books in the Polish language were published, contributing to increased homogeneity of grammar and orthography.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-45) The writing system achieved its overall form in the 16th century,[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-Kolaczyk-35)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKamusella2009111-46) which is also regarded as the "[Golden Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_Golden_Age "Polish Golden Age") of Polish literature".[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-Comrie-43) The [orthography was modified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Polish_orthography "History of Polish orthography") in the 19th century and in 1936.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-Kolaczyk-35)

[Tomasz Kamusella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomasz_Kamusella "Tomasz Kamusella") notes that "Polish is the oldest, non-ecclesiastical, written Slavic language with a continuous tradition of literacy and official use, which has lasted unbroken from the 16th century to this day."[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-47) Polish evolved into the main [sociolect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sociolect "Sociolect") of the nobles in [Poland–Lithuania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish%E2%80%93Lithuanian_union "Polish–Lithuanian union") in the 15th century.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKamusella2009111-46) The history of Polish as a language of state governance begins in the 16th century in the [Kingdom of Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_of_the_Kingdom_of_Poland "Crown of the Kingdom of Poland"). Over the later centuries, Polish served as the official language in the [Grand Duchy of Lithuania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Duchy_of_Lithuania "Grand Duchy of Lithuania"), [Congress Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congress_Poland "Congress Poland"), the [Kingdom of Galicia and Lodomeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Galicia_and_Lodomeria "Kingdom of Galicia and Lodomeria"), and as the administrative language in the [Russian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Empire "Russian Empire")'s [Western Krai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Krai "Western Krai"). The growth of the [Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish%E2%80%93Lithuanian_Commonwealth "Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth")'s influence gave Polish the status of _lingua franca_ in [Central and Eastern Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_and_Eastern_Europe "Central and Eastern Europe").[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKamusella2009137-48)

The process of standardization began in the 14th century[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-49) and solidified in the 16th century during the Middle Polish era.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-Dejna-33):16–17 Standard Polish was based on various dialectal features, with the [Greater Poland dialect group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Poland_dialect_group "Greater Poland dialect group") serving as the base.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-Dejna-33):18 After [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), Standard Polish became the most widely spoken variant of Polish across the country, and most dialects stopped being the form of Polish spoken in villages.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-50)

## Geographic distribution

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Polish_language&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Geographic distribution")]

See also: [Geographical distribution of Polish speakers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geographical_distribution_of_Polish_speakers "Geographical distribution of Polish speakers")

Poland is one of the most linguistically [homogeneous](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/homogeneous "wiktionary:homogeneous") European countries; nearly 97% of Poland's citizens declare Polish as their [first language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_language "First language"). Elsewhere, [Poles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_people "Polish people") constitute large minorities in areas which were once administered or occupied by Poland, notably in neighboring [Lithuania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithuania "Lithuania"), [Belarus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belarus "Belarus"), and [Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukraine "Ukraine"). Polish is the most widely used minority language in Lithuania's [Vilnius County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vilnius_County "Vilnius County"), by 26% of the population, according to the 2001 census results, as [Vilnius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vilnius "Vilnius") was part of Poland from 1922 until 1939. Polish is found elsewhere in southeastern Lithuania. In Ukraine, it is most common in the western parts of [Lviv](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lviv_Oblast "Lviv Oblast") and [Volyn Oblasts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volyn_Oblast "Volyn Oblast"), while in [West Belarus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Belarus "West Belarus") it is used by the significant Polish minority, especially in the [Brest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brest,_Belarus "Brest, Belarus") and [Grodno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grodno "Grodno") regions and in areas along the Lithuanian border. There are significant numbers of Polish speakers among Polish emigrants and their descendants in many other countries.

In the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"), [Polish Americans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_Americans "Polish Americans") number more than 11 million but most of them cannot speak Polish fluently. According to the [2000 United States census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_United_States_census "2000 United States census"), 667,414  Americans of age five years and over reported Polish as the language spoken at home, which is about 1.4% of people who speak languages other than [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_language "English language"), 0.25% of the US population, and 6% of the Polish-American population. The largest concentrations of Polish speakers reported in the census (over 50%) were found in three states: [Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois "Illinois") (185,749), [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state) "New York (state)") (111,740), and [New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jersey "New Jersey") (74,663).[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-51) Enough people in these areas speak Polish that [PNC Financial Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PNC_Financial_Services "PNC Financial Services") (which has a large number of branches in all of these areas) offers services available in Polish at all of their [cash machines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cash_machine "Cash machine") in addition to [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_language "English language") and [Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language").[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-52)

According to the 2011 census there are now over 500,000 people in [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England "England") and [Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wales "Wales") who consider Polish to be their "main" language. In [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada"), there is a significant [Polish Canadian population](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_Canadians "Polish Canadians"): There are 242,885 speakers of Polish according to the 2006 census; in particular, there are concentrations of Polish speakers in [Toronto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto "Toronto") (91,810 speakers) and [Montreal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montreal "Montreal").[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-census-53)

The geographical distribution of the Polish language was greatly affected by the [territorial changes of Poland immediately after World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Territorial_changes_of_Poland_immediately_after_World_War_II "Territorial changes of Poland immediately after World War II") and [Polish population transfers (1944–46)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_population_transfers_(1944%E2%80%9346) "Polish population transfers (1944–46)"). Poles settled in the "[Recovered Territories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recovered_Territories "Recovered Territories")" in the west and north, which had previously been mostly [German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_language "German language")-speaking. Some Poles remained in the previously Polish-ruled territories in the east that were annexed by the [USSR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union"), resulting in the present-day Polish-speaking communities in Lithuania, Belarus, and Ukraine, although many Poles were expelled from those areas to areas within Poland's new borders. To the east of Poland, the most significant Polish minority lives in a long strip along either side of the [Lithuania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithuania "Lithuania")-[Belarus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belarus "Belarus") border. Meanwhile, the [flight and expulsion of Germans (1944–50)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flight_and_expulsion_of_Germans_(1944%E2%80%9350) "Flight and expulsion of Germans (1944–50)"), as well as the [expulsion of Ukrainians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Population_exchange_between_Poland_and_Soviet_Ukraine "Population exchange between Poland and Soviet Ukraine") and [Operation Vistula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Vistula "Operation Vistula"), the 1947 migration of Ukrainian minorities in the Recovered Territories in the west of the country, contributed to the country's linguistic homogeneity.

## Dialects

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Polish_language&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Dialects")]

Main article: [Dialects of Polish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dialects_of_Polish "Dialects of Polish")

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3b/Modlitwy_drukowane_po_polsku_w_r._1475.JPG/250px-Modlitwy_drukowane_po_polsku_w_r._1475.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Modlitwy_drukowane_po_polsku_w_r._1475.JPG)

The oldest printed text in Polish – _Statuta synodalia Episcoporum Wratislaviensis_ printed in 1475 in [Wrocław](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wroc%C5%82aw "Wrocław") by Kasper Elyan.

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c3/Polish-alphabet.png/250px-Polish-alphabet.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Polish-alphabet.png)

The Polish alphabet contains 32 letters. Q, V and X are not used in the Polish language.

The inhabitants of different regions of Poland still[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Polish_language&action=edit) speak Polish somewhat differently, although the differences between modern-day [vernacular](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vernacular "Vernacular") varieties and standard Polish (_język ogólnopolski_) appear relatively slight. Most of the middle aged and young speak vernaculars close to standard Polish, while the traditional dialects are preserved among older people in rural areas.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-wtad-54) First-language speakers of Polish have no trouble understanding each other, and non-native speakers may have difficulty recognizing the regional and [social](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sociolect "Sociolect") differences. The modern [standard dialect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_language "Standard language"), often termed as "correct Polish",[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-wtad-54) is spoken or at least understood throughout the entire country.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-Swan-2002-25)

Polish has traditionally been described as consisting of three to five main regional dialects:

*   [Greater Polish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Polish_dialect "Greater Polish dialect"), spoken in the west
*   [Lesser Polish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lesser_Polish_dialect "Lesser Polish dialect"), spoken in the south and southeast
*   [Masovian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masovian_dialect "Masovian dialect"), spoken throughout the central and eastern parts of the country

[Silesian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silesian_language "Silesian language") and [Kashubian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kashubian_language "Kashubian language"), spoken in [Upper Silesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_Silesia "Upper Silesia") and [Pomerania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pomerania "Pomerania") respectively, are thought of as either [Polish dialects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dialects_of_Polish "Dialects of Polish") or [distinct languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ausbau "Ausbau"), depending on the criteria used.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-55)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-56)

Kashubian contains a number of features not found elsewhere in Poland, e.g. nine distinct oral vowels (vs. the six of standard Polish) and (in the northern dialects) phonemic word stress, an archaic feature preserved from [Common Slavic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_Slavic "Common Slavic") times and not found anywhere else among the [West Slavic languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Slavic_languages "West Slavic languages"). However, it was described by some linguists as lacking most of the linguistic and social determinants of language-hood.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-57)

Many linguistic sources categorize Silesian as a regional language separate from Polish,[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-58) while some consider Silesian to be a dialect of Polish.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-59) Many Silesians consider themselves a separate ethnicity and have been advocating for the recognition of Silesian as a [regional language in Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Languages_of_Poland "Languages of Poland"). The law recognizing it as such was passed by the [Sejm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sejm "Sejm") and [Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_of_Poland "Senate of Poland") in April 2024, but was vetoed by President [Andrzej Duda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrzej_Duda "Andrzej Duda") in late May 2024.

According to the last official census in Poland in 2011, over half a million people declared Silesian as their native language. Many sociolinguists (e.g. [Tomasz Kamusella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomasz_Kamusella "Tomasz Kamusella"),[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-60) Agnieszka Pianka, Alfred F. Majewicz,[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-61)[Tomasz Wicherkiewicz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomasz_Wicherkiewicz "Tomasz Wicherkiewicz"))[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-62) assume that extralinguistic criteria decide whether a lect is an independent language or a dialect: speakers of the [speech variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety_(linguistics) "Variety (linguistics)") or/and political decisions, and this is dynamic (i.e. it changes over time). Also, research organizations such as [SIL International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIL_International "SIL International")[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-SIL-63) and resources for the academic field of linguistics such as _[Ethnologue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnologue "Ethnologue")_,[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-64)[Linguist List](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linguist_List "Linguist List")[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-65) and others, for example the [Ministry of Administration and Digitization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Administration_and_Digitization_(Poland) "Ministry of Administration and Digitization (Poland)")[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-MoAaD-66) recognized the Silesian language. In July 2007, the Silesian language was recognized by [ISO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Organization_for_Standardization "International Organization for Standardization"), and was attributed an ISO code of szl.

Some additional characteristic but less widespread regional dialects include:

1.   The distinctive dialect of the [Gorals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gorals#Language "Gorals") (_Góralski_) occurs in the mountainous area bordering the [Czech Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Czech_Republic "Czech Republic") and [Slovakia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovakia "Slovakia"). The Gorals ("Highlanders") take great pride in their culture and the dialect. It exhibits some cultural influences from the [Vlach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vlachs "Vlachs") shepherds in the 14th–17th centuries.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-67)
2.   The [Poznański dialect](https://pl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gwara%20pozna%C5%84ska "pl:Gwara poznańska"), spoken in [Poznań](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pozna%C5%84 "Poznań") and to some extent in the whole region of the former [Prussian Partition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prussian_Partition "Prussian Partition") (excluding [Upper Silesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_Silesia "Upper Silesia")), with noticeable German influences.
3.   In the northern and western (formerly German) regions where Poles from the territories annexed by the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union") resettled after World War II, the older generation speaks a dialect of Polish characteristic of the [Kresy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kresy "Kresy") that includes a longer pronunciation of vowels.
4.   Poles living in [Lithuania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithuania "Lithuania") (particularly in the [Vilnius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vilnius "Vilnius") region), in Belarus (particularly the northwest), and in the northeast of Poland continue to speak the [Eastern Borderlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kresy "Kresy") dialect, which sounds "slushed"[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please\_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_] (in Polish described as _zaciąganie z ruska_, "speaking with a Ruthenian drawl") and is easily distinguishable.
5.   Some city dwellers, especially the less affluent population, had their own distinctive dialects – for example, the [Warsaw dialect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warsaw_dialect "Warsaw dialect"), still spoken by some of the population of [Praga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Praga "Praga") on the eastern bank of the [Vistula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vistula "Vistula"). However, these city dialects are now[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Polish_language&action=edit) mostly extinct due to assimilation with standard Polish.
6.   Many Poles living in emigrant communities (for example, in [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil "Brazil") and the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States")), whose families left Poland during the 20th century, retain a number of minor features of Polish vocabulary as spoken in the first half of that century that now sound archaic to contemporary visitors from Poland.

Polish linguistics has been characterized by a strong strive towards promoting [prescriptive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linguistic_prescription "Linguistic prescription") ideas of language intervention and usage uniformity,[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-mling-68) along with normatively oriented notions of language "correctness"[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-wtad-54) (unusual by Western standards).[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-mling-68)

### Vowels

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Polish_language&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Vowels")]

Polish has six oral vowels (seven oral vowels in written form), which are all [monophthongs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monophthong "Monophthong"), and two [nasal vowels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasal_vowel "Nasal vowel").[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-69) The oral vowels are /[i](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Close_front_unrounded_vowel "Close front unrounded vowel")/ (spelled _i_), /[ɨ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Close-mid_central_unrounded_vowel "Close-mid central unrounded vowel")/ (spelled _y_ and also transcribed as /ɘ/ or /ɪ/), /[ɛ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open-mid_front_unrounded_vowel "Open-mid front unrounded vowel")/ (spelled _e_), /[a](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_front_unrounded_vowel "Open front unrounded vowel")/ (spelled _a_), /[ɔ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open-mid_back_rounded_vowel "Open-mid back rounded vowel")/ (spelled _o_) and /[u](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Close_back_rounded_vowel "Close back rounded vowel")/ (spelled _u_ and _[ó](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%93 "Ó")_ as separate letters). The nasal vowels are /[ɛ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open-mid_front_unrounded_vowel "Open-mid front unrounded vowel")[w̃](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasal_labial%E2%80%93velar_approximant "Nasal labial–velar approximant")/ (spelled _[ę](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C4%98 "Ę")_) and /[ɔ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open-mid_back_rounded_vowel "Open-mid back rounded vowel")[w̃](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasal_labial%E2%80%93velar_approximant "Nasal labial–velar approximant")/ (spelled _[ą](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C4%84 "Ą")_).[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-70) Unlike Czech or Slovak, Polish does not retain phonemic vowel length — the letter _ó_, which formerly represented lengthened /ɔː/ in older forms of the language, is now vestigial and instead corresponds to /u/.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-71)

For details, see _[Voicing and devoicing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish\_phonology#Voicing\_and\_devoicing "Polish phonology")_ in the article on Polish phonology.

Most Polish words are [paroxytones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paroxytone "Paroxytone") (that is, the [stress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stress_(linguistics) "Stress (linguistics)") falls on the second-to-last syllable of a polysyllabic word), although there are exceptions.

### Consonant distribution

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Polish_language&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Consonant distribution")]

Polish permits complex consonant clusters, which historically often arose from the disappearance of [yers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yer "Yer"). Polish can have word-initial and word-medial clusters of up to four consonants, whereas word-final clusters can have up to five consonants.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-72) Examples of such clusters can be found in words such as [_bezwzględny_](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/9/9b/Pl-bezwzgl%C4%99dny.ogg/Pl-bezwzgl%C4%99dny.ogg.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pl-bezwzgl%C4%99dny.ogg "File:Pl-bezwzględny.ogg")[bɛzˈvzɡlɛndnɨ] ('absolute' or 'heartless', 'ruthless'), [_źdźbło_](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/3/38/Pl-%C5%BAd%C5%BAb%C5%82o.ogg/Pl-%C5%BAd%C5%BAb%C5%82o.ogg.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pl-%C5%BAd%C5%BAb%C5%82o.ogg "File:Pl-źdźbło.ogg")[ˈʑd͡ʑbwɔ] ('blade of grass'), [_wstrząs_](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/2/26/Pl-wstrz%C4%85s.ogg/Pl-wstrz%C4%85s.ogg.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pl-wstrz%C4%85s.ogg "File:Pl-wstrząs.ogg")[ˈfstʂɔw̃s] ('shock'), and _krnąbrność_[ˈkrnɔmbrnɔɕt͡ɕ] ('disobedience'). A popular Polish [tongue-twister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tongue-twister "Tongue-twister") (from a verse by [Jan Brzechwa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Brzechwa "Jan Brzechwa")) is [_W Szczebrzeszynie chrząszcz brzmi w trzcinie_](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/2/22/Polish_Tongue_twister_-_Chrz%C4%85szcz_-_2.ogg/Polish_Tongue_twister_-_Chrz%C4%85szcz_-_2.ogg.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Polish_Tongue_twister_-_Chrz%C4%85szcz_-_2.ogg "File:Polish Tongue twister - Chrząszcz - 2.ogg")[fʂt͡ʂɛbʐɛˈʂɨɲɛ ˈxʂɔw̃ʂt͡ʂ ˈbʐmi fˈtʂt͡ɕiɲɛ] ('In [Szczebrzeszyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Szczebrzeszyn "Szczebrzeszyn") a beetle buzzes in the reed').

Unlike languages such as Czech, Polish does not have [syllabic consonants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syllabic_consonant "Syllabic consonant") – the nucleus of a [syllable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syllable "Syllable") is always a vowel.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-73)

The consonant /j/ is restricted to positions adjacent to a vowel. It also cannot precede or follow the letter Y.

### Prosody

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Polish_language&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Prosody")]

The predominant [stress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stress_(linguistics) "Stress (linguistics)") pattern in Polish is penultimate stress – in a word of more than one syllable, the next-to-last syllable is stressed. Alternating preceding syllables carry secondary stress, e.g. in a four-syllable word, where the primary stress is on the third syllable, there will be secondary stress on the first.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-74)

Each vowel represents one syllable, although the letter _i_ normally does not represent a vowel when it precedes another vowel (it represents /j/, palatalization of the preceding consonant, or both depending on analysis). Also the letters _u_ and _i_ sometimes represent only semivowels when they follow another vowel, as in _autor_/ˈawtɔr/ ('author'), mostly in loanwords (so not in native _nauka_/naˈu.ka/ 'science, the act of learning', for example, nor in nativized _Mateusz_/maˈte.uʂ/ 'Matthew').

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b0/Styl_urzedowy_-_Polish_sign.jpg/250px-Styl_urzedowy_-_Polish_sign.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Styl_urzedowy_-_Polish_sign.jpg)

A formal-tone informative sign in Polish, with a composition of vowels and consonants and a mixture of long, medium and short [syllables](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syllables "Syllables")

Some [loanwords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loanword "Loanword"), particularly from the [classical languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_language "Classical language"), have the stress on the antepenultimate (third-from-last) syllable. For example, _fizyka_ (/ˈfizɨka/) ('physics') is stressed on the first syllable. This may lead to a rare phenomenon of minimal pairs differing only in stress placement, for example _muzyka_/ˈmuzɨka/ 'music' vs. _muzyka_/muˈzɨka/ – genitive singular of _muzyk_ 'musician'. When additional syllables are added to such words through [inflection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inflection "Inflection") or [suffixation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suffix "Suffix"), the stress normally becomes regular. For example, _uniwersytet_ (/uɲiˈvɛrsɨtɛt/, 'university') has irregular stress on the third (or antepenultimate) syllable, but the genitive _uniwersytetu_ (/uɲivɛrsɨˈtɛtu/) and derived adjective _uniwersytecki_ (/uɲivɛrsɨˈtɛt͡skʲi/) have regular stress on the penultimate syllables. Loanwords generally become nativized to have penultimate stress.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGussmann20079-75) In psycholinguistic experiments, speakers of Polish have been demonstrated to be sensitive to the distinction between regular penultimate and exceptional antepenultimate stress.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-76)

Another class of exceptions is verbs with the conditional endings _-by, -bym, -byśmy_, etc. These endings are not counted in determining the position of the stress; for example, _**zro**biłbym_ ('I would do') is stressed on the first syllable, and _zro**bi**libyśmy_ ('we would do') on the second. According to [prescriptive authorities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linguistic_prescription "Linguistic prescription"), the same applies to the first and second person plural past tense endings _-śmy, -ście_, although this rule is often ignored in [colloquial speech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colloquialism "Colloquialism") (so _zro**bi**liśmy_ 'we did' should be prescriptively stressed on the second syllable, although in [practice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Usus "Usus") it is commonly stressed on the third as _zrobi**li**śmy_).[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-77) These irregular stress patterns are explained by the fact that these endings are detachable [clitics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clitic "Clitic") rather than true verbal inflections: for example, instead of _**ko**go zoba**czy**liście?_ ('whom did you see?') it is possible to say _**ko**goście zoba**czy**li?_ – here _kogo_ retains its usual stress (first syllable) in spite of the attachment of the clitic. Reanalysis of the endings as inflections when attached to verbs causes the different colloquial stress patterns. These stress patterns are considered part of a "usable" norm of standard Polish - in contrast to the "model" ("high") norm.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-78)

Some common word combinations are stressed as if they were a single word. This applies in particular to many combinations of preposition plus a personal pronoun, such as _**do** niej_ ('to her'), _**na** nas_ ('on us'), _prze**ze** mnie_ ('because of me'), all stressed on the bolded syllable.

## Orthography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Polish_language&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Orthography")]

Main articles: [Polish orthography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_orthography "Polish orthography") and [Polish Braille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_Braille "Polish Braille")

See also: [History of Polish orthography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Polish_orthography "History of Polish orthography")

The [Polish alphabet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_alphabet "Polish alphabet") derives from the [Latin script](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_script "Latin script") but includes certain additional letters formed using [diacritics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diacritic "Diacritic"). The Polish alphabet was one of three major forms of Latin-based orthography developed for Western and some South Slavic languages, the others being [Czech orthography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Czech_orthography "Czech orthography") and [Croatian orthography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Croatian_language "Croatian language"), the last of these being a 19th-century invention trying to make a compromise between the first two. [Kashubian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kashubian_language "Kashubian language") uses a Polish-based system, [Slovak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovak_language "Slovak language") uses a Czech-based system, and [Slovene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovene_language "Slovene language") follows the Croatian one; the [Sorbian languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sorbian_languages "Sorbian languages") blend the Polish and the Czech ones.

Historically, Poland's once diverse and multi-ethnic population utilized many forms of scripture to write Polish. For instance, [Lipka Tatars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lipka_Tatars "Lipka Tatars") and [Muslims](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslims "Muslims") inhabiting the eastern parts of the former [Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish%E2%80%93Lithuanian_Commonwealth "Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth") wrote Polish in the [Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic_alphabet "Arabic alphabet") alphabet.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-79) The [Cyrillic script](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyrillic_script "Cyrillic script") is used to a certain extent today by [Polish speakers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poles_in_Belarus "Poles in Belarus") in [Western Belarus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Belarus "Western Belarus"), especially for religious texts.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-80)

The diacritics used in the Polish alphabet are the _kreska_ (graphically similar to the [acute accent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acute_accent "Acute accent")) over the letters _ć, ń, ó, ś, ź_ and through the letter in _ł_; the _kropka_ (superior dot) over the letter _ż_, and the _[ogonek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ogonek "Ogonek")_ ("little tail") under the letters _ą, ę_. The letters _q, v, x_ are used only in foreign words and names.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language#cite_note-sjp.pwn.pl-19)

Polish orthography is largely [phonemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoneme "Phoneme")—there is a consistent correspondence between letters (or [digraphs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digraph_(orthography) "Digraph (orthography)") and [trigraphs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trigraph_(orthography) "Trigraph (orthography)")) and phonemes (for exceptions see below). Voiced consonant letters frequently come to represent voiceless sounds (as shown in the tables); this occurs at the end of words and in certain clusters, due to the neutralization mentioned in the _[Phonology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish\_language#Phonology)_ section above. Occasionally also voiceless consonant letters can represent voiced sounds in clusters.

The spelling rule for the palatal sounds /[ɕ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceless_alveolo-palatal_fricative "Voiceless alveolo-palatal fricative")/, /[ʑ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiced_alveolo-palatal_fricative "Voiced alveolo-palatal fricative")/, /[tɕ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceless_alveolo-palatal_affricate "Voiceless alveolo-palatal affricate")/, /[dʑ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiced_alveolo-palatal_affricate "Voiced alveolo-palatal affricate")/ and /[ɲ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiced_alveolo-palatal_nasal "Voiced alveolo-palatal nasal")/ is as follows: before the vowel _i_ the plain letters _s, z, c, dz, n_ are used; before other vowels the combinations _si, zi, ci, dzi, ni_ are used; when not followed by a vowel the diacritic forms _ś, ź, ć, dź, ń_ are used. For example, the _s_ in _siwy_ ("grey-haired"), the _si_ in _siarka_ ("sulfur") and the _ś_ in _święty_ ("holy") all represent the sound /[ɕ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceless_alveolo-palatal_fricative "Voiceless alveolo-palatal fricative")/. The exceptions to the above rule are certain loanwords from Latin, Italian, French, Russian or English—where _s_ before _i_ is pronounced as _s_, e.g. _sinus_, _sinologia_, _do re mi fa sol la si do_, _Saint-Simon i saint-simoniści_, _Sierioża_, _Siergiej_, _Singapur_, _singiel_. In other loanwords the vowel _i_ is changed to _y_, e.g. _asymilacja_.

| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| /[tɕ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceless_alveolo-palatal_affricate "Voiceless alveolo-palatal affricate")/ | _ć_ | _ci_ | _c_ |
| /[dʑ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiced_alveolo-palatal_affricate "Voiced alveolo-palatal affricate")/ | _dź_ | _dzi_ | _dz_ |

Similar principles apply to /[kʲ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palatalization_(phonetics) "Palatalization (phonetics)")/, /[ɡʲ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palatalization_(phonetics) "Palatalization (phonetics)")/, /[xʲ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palatalization_(phonetics) "Palatalization (phonetics)")/ and [/lʲ/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palatalization_(phonetics) "Palatalization (phonetics)"), except that these can only occur before vowels, so the spellings are _k, g, (c)h, l_ before _i_, and _ki, gi, (c)hi, li_ otherwise. Most Polish speakers, however, do not consider palatalization of _k, g, (c)h_ or _l_ as creating new sounds.

Except in the cases mentioned above, the letter _i_ if followed by another vowel in the same word usually represents /[j](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiced_palatal_approximant "Voiced palatal approximant")/, yet a palatalization of the previous consonant is always assumed.

The reverse case, where the consonant remains unpalatalized but is followed by a palatalized consonant, is written by using _j_ instead of _i_: for example, _zjeść_, "to eat up".

The letters _ą_ and _ę_, when followed by plosives and affricates, represent an oral vowel followed by a nasal consonant, rather than a nasal vowel. For example, _ą_ in _dąb_ ("oak") is pronounced [[ɔm]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Polish "Help:IPA/Polish"), and _ę_ in _tęcza_ ("rainbow") is pronounced [[ɛn]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Polish "Help:IPA/Polish") (the nasal assimilates to the following consonant). When followed by _l_ or _ł_ (for example _przyjęli_, _przyjęły_), _ę_ is pronounced as just _e_. When _ę_ is at the end of the word it is often pronounced as just [[ɛ]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Polish "Help:IPA/Polish").

Depending on the word, the phoneme /[x](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiceless_velar_fricative "Voiceless velar fricative")/ can be spelt _h_ or _ch_, the phoneme /[ʐ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiced_retroflex_fricative "Voiced retroflex fricative")/ can be spelt _ż_ or _rz_, and /[u](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Close_back_rounded_vowel "Close back rounded vowel")/ can be spelt _u_ or _ó_. In several cases it determines the meaning, for example: _może_ ("maybe") and _morze_ ("sea").

In occasional words, letters that normally form a digraph are pronounced separately. For example, _rz_ represents /rz/, not /[ʐ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiced_retroflex_fricative "Voiced retroflex fricative")/, in words like _zamarzać_ ("freeze") and in the name _\_[Tarzan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarzan "Tarzan")\__.

Doubled letters are usually pronounced as a single, [lengthened](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gemination#Polish "Gemination") consonant, however, some speakers might pronounce the combination as two separate sounds.

There are certain clusters where a written consonant would not be pronounced. For example, the _ł_ in the word _jabłko_ ("apple") might be omitted in ordinary speech, leading to the pronunciation _japko_.

## Grammar

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Polish_language&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Grammar")]

Main article: [Polish grammar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_grammar "Polish grammar")

[![Image 15: icon](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/9/99/Question_book-new.svg/60px-Question_book-new.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Question_book-new.svg)This section **does not [cite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources") any [sources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")**. Unsourced material may be challenged and [removed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Burden_of_evidence "Wikipedia:Verifiability")._(January 2026)_ _([Learn how and when to remove this message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Maintenance\_template\_removal "Help:Maintenance template removal"))_

Polish is a highly [fusional language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fusional_language "Fusional language") with relatively free [word order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word_order "Word order"), although the dominant arrangement is [subject–verb–object](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subject%E2%80%93verb%E2%80%93object "Subject–verb–object") (SVO). There are no [articles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Article_(grammar) "Article (grammar)"), and subject pronouns are often [dropped](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pro-drop_language "Pro-drop language").

[Nouns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noun "Noun") belong to one of three [genders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammatical_gender "Grammatical gender"): masculine, feminine and neuter. The masculine gender is also divided into subgenders: animate vs inanimate in the singular, human vs nonhuman in the plural. There are seven [cases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Case_(grammar) "Case (grammar)"): nominative, genitive, dative, accusative, instrumental, locative and vocative.

[Adjectives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adjective "Adjective") agree with nouns in terms of gender, case, and number. [Attributive adjectives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attributive_adjective "Attributive adjective") most commonly precede the noun, although in certain cases, especially in fixed phrases (like _język polski_, "Polish (language)"), the noun may come first; the rule of thumb is that generic descriptive adjectives normally precede (e.g. _piękny kwiat_, "beautiful flower") while categorizing adjectives often follow the noun (e.g. _węgiel kamienny_, "black coal"). Most short adjectives and their derived [adverbs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adverb "Adverb") form [comparatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comparative "Comparative") and [superlatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superlative "Superlative") by inflection (the superlative is formed by prefixing _naj-_ to the comparative).

[Verbs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verb "Verb") are of imperfective or perfective [aspect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aspect_(grammar) "Aspect (grammar)"), often occurring in pairs. Imperfective verbs have a present tense, past tense, compound future tense (except for _być_ "to be", which has a simple future _będę_ etc., this in turn being used to form the compound future of other verbs), subjunctive/conditional (formed with the detachable particle _by_), imperatives, an infinitive, present participle, present gerund and past participle. Perfective verbs have a simple future tense (formed like the present tense of imperfective verbs), past tense, subjunctive/conditional, imperatives, infinitive, present gerund and past participle. Conjugated verb forms agree with their subject in terms of person, number, and (in the case of past tense and subjunctive/conditional forms) gender.

[Passive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passive_voice "Passive voice")-type constructions can be made using the auxiliary _być_ or _zostać_ ("become") with the passive participle. There is also an impersonal construction where the active verb is used (in third person singular) with no subject, but with the reflexive pronoun _się_ present to indicate a general, unspecified subject (as in _pije się wódkę_ "vodka is being drunk"—note that _wódka_ appears in the accusative). A similar sentence type in the past tense uses the passive participle with the ending _-o_, as in _widziano ludzi_ ("people were seen"). As in other Slavic languages, there are also subjectless sentences formed using such words as _można_ ("it is possible") together with an infinitive.

[Yes–no questions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes%E2%80%93no_question "Yes–no question") (both direct and indirect) are formed by placing the word _czy_ ("whether") at the start, although it's often omitted in casual speech. Negation uses the word _nie_, before the verb or other item being negated; _nie_ is still added before the verb even if the sentence also contains other negatives such as _nigdy_ ("never") or _nic_ ("nothing"), effectively creating a [double negative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_negative "Double negative").

[Cardinal numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_number_(linguistics) "Cardinal number (linguistics)") have a complex system of inflection and agreement. Zero and cardinal numbers higher than five (except for those ending with the digit 2, 3 or 4 but not ending with 12, 13 or 14) govern the [genitive case](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genitive_case "Genitive case") rather than the nominative or accusative. Special forms of numbers ([collective numerals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collective_numeral "Collective numeral")) are used with certain classes of noun, which include _dziecko_ ("child") and [exclusively plural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plurale_tantum "Plurale tantum") nouns such as _drzwi_ ("door").
