Poland has a social market economy and is a regional economic power in East-Central Europe.[272] As of 2025, the country's gross domestic product (GDP) is the sixth largest in the European Union by nominal standards, the fifth largest by purchasing power parity, and ranks 20th globally.[273] It is one of the fastest growing within the Union and reached a developed market status in 2018.[274] The unemployment rate published by Eurostat in 2023 amounted to 2.8%, which was the second-lowest in the EU.[275] As of 2023, around 62% of the employed population works in the service sector, 29% in manufacturing, and 8% in the agricultural sector, thus manifesting a highly diversified economy.[276] Although Poland is a member of the European single market, the country has not adopted the Euro as legal tender and maintains its own currency – the Polish złoty (zł, PLN).[277]

Gdańsk, located on the Baltic in the north of Poland, is a major seaport as well as an economic and tourist zone.

Poland is a regional European leader in terms of foreign direct investment[278] and possesses around 40 percent of the 500 biggest companies in the region by revenues whilst maintaining a high globalisation rate and relatively high economic competitiveness.[279][280] The country's largest firms compose the WIG20 and WIG30 stock market indexes, which are traded on the Warsaw Stock Exchange.[281] The Central Statistical Office estimated that in 2014 there were 1,437 Polish corporations with interests in 3,194 foreign entities.[282] Poland also has the largest banking sector in East-Central Europe,[283] with 32.3 branches per 100,000 adults.[284] The monetary policy is determined by the National Bank of Poland (NBP), which controls the issuing of the national currency.[277] It was the only European economy to have avoided the recession of 2008.[285] Since 2019, workers under the age of 26 are exempt from paying the income tax.[286]

The country is the 19th largest exporter of goods and services in the world.[287] Exports of goods and services are valued at approximately 58% of GDP, as of 2023.[288] Poland's largest trade partners are Germany, the United Kingdom, the Czech Republic, France, Italy, the Netherlands, and the United States.[289] Among its lead exports are motor cars, buses, and vehicle-related accessories, machinery, electronics, electric batteries, home appliances, furniture, cosmetics, military equipment, and tobacco as well as materials such as silver, copper, steel, coal, zinc, tar, and coke.[289] In 2023, the country produced 1300 tonnes of silver and was the 5th largest silver producer globally.[290] As of May 2026, Poland holds the world's 11th largest gold reserve, estimated at 582 tonnes.[291]

Tourism
Main article: Tourism in Poland
Malbork Castle is the largest castle in the world measured by land area and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

In 2020, the total value of the tourism industry in Poland was 104.3 billion PLN, then equivalent to 4.5% of the Polish GDP.[292] Tourism contributes considerably to the overall economy and makes up a relatively large proportion of the country's service market.[293] Nearly 200,000 people were employed in the accommodation and catering (hospitality) sector in 2020.[292] In 2021, Poland ranked 12th most visited country in the world by international arrivals.[294]

Tourist attractions in Poland range from the mountains in the south to the beaches on the Baltic Sea in the north. Many trail of rich architectural and cultural heritage. Among the most recognisable landmarks are Old Towns in Kraków, Warsaw, Wrocław (dwarf statues), Gdańsk, Poznań, Lublin, Toruń and Zamość as well as museums, zoological gardens, theme parks and the Wieliczka Salt Mine, with its labyrinthine tunnels, underground lake and chapels carved by miners out of rock salt beneath the ground. There are over 100 castles in the country, largely within the Lower Silesian Voivodeship (including the Piast Castles Trail), and also on the Trail of the Eagles' Nests; the largest castle in the world by land area is situated in Malbork.[295][296] The German Auschwitz concentration camp in Oświęcim, and the Skull Chapel in Kudowa-Zdrój constitute dark tourism.[297] Regarding nature based travel, notable sites include the Masurian Lake District and Białowieża Forest in the east; on the south Karkonosze, the Table Mountains, the Pieniny and the Tatra Mountains, where Rysy and the Eagle's Path trail are located. The Bieszczady Mountains lie in the extreme south-east.[298]

Transport
Main article: Transport in Poland
PKP Intercity Pendolino at Wrocław Główny railway station

Transport in Poland is provided by means of rail, road, marine shipping and air travel. The country is part of EU's Schengen Area and is an important transport hub due to its strategic geographical position in Central Europe.[299] Some of the longest European routes, including the E30 and E40, run through Poland. The country has a good network of highways consisting of express roads and motorways. As of August 2023, Poland has the world's 21st-largest road network, maintaining over 5,000 km (3,100 mi) of highways in use.[300] In larger cities, public transport is heavily utilised; Poland is one of Europe's largest bus and tram manufacturers, and hosts one of the biggest tram and light rail transit systems.[301]

In 2022, the nation had 19,393 kilometres (12,050 mi) of railway track, the third longest in the European Union after Germany and France.[302] Polish State Railways (PKP) is the dominant railway operator, with certain major voivodeships or urban areas possessing their own commuter and regional rail.[303] Poland has a number of international airports, the largest of which is Warsaw Chopin Airport.[304] It is the primary global hub for LOT Polish Airlines, the country's flag carrier.[305]

Seaports exist all along Poland's Baltic coast, with most freight operations using Świnoujście, Police, Szczecin, Kołobrzeg, Gdynia, Gdańsk and Elbląg as their base. The Port of Gdańsk is the only port in the Baltic Sea adapted to receive oceanic vessels. Polferries and Unity Line are the largest Polish ferry operators, with the latter providing roll-on/roll-off and train ferry services to Scandinavia.[306]

Energy
Main article: Energy in Poland
Share of electricity generation in Poland - percentage share

The electricity generation sector in Poland is largely fossil-fuel–based. Coal production in Poland is a major source of employment and the largest source of the nation's greenhouse gas emissions.[307] Many power plants nationwide use Poland's position as a major European exporter of coal to their advantage by continuing to use coal as the primary raw material in the production of their energy. The three largest Polish coal mining firms (Węglokoks, Kompania Węglowa and JSW) extract around 100 million tonnes of coal annually.[308] After coal, Polish energy supply relies significantly on natural gas and oil.

The new Energy Policy of Poland until 2040 (EPP2040) would reduce the share of coal and lignite in electricity generation by 25% from 2017 to 2030. The plan involves deploying new nuclear plants, increasing energy efficiency, and decarbonising the Polish transport system in order to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and prioritise long-term energy security.[307][309] In March 2026, PEJ submitted an application for a permit to build a nuclear power plant.

Science and technology
Main articles: Timeline of Polish science and technology and List of Polish Nobel laureates
Physicist and chemist Maria Skłodowska-Curie was the first person to win two Nobel Prizes.[310]
Astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus formulated the heliocentric model of the Solar System.

Over the course of history, the Polish people have made considerable contributions in the fields of science, technology and mathematics.[311] Perhaps the most renowned Pole to support this theory was Nicolaus Copernicus, who triggered the Copernican Revolution by placing the Sun rather than the Earth at the centre of the universe.[312] He also derived a quantity theory of money, which made him a pioneer of economics. Copernicus' achievements and discoveries are considered the basis of Polish culture and cultural identity.[313] Poland was ranked 39th in the Global Innovation Index in 2025.[314][315]

Poland's tertiary education institutions; traditional universities, as well as technical, medical, and economic institutions, employ around tens of thousands of researchers and staff members. There are hundreds of research and development institutes.[316] However, in the 19th and 20th centuries many Polish scientists worked abroad; one of the most important of these exiles was Maria Skłodowska-Curie, a physicist and chemist who lived much of her life in France. In 1925, she established Poland's Radium Institute.[310]

In the first half of the 20th century, Poland was a flourishing centre of mathematics. Outstanding Polish mathematicians formed the Lwów School of Mathematics (with Stefan Banach, Stanisław Mazur, Hugo Steinhaus, Stanisław Ulam) and Warsaw School of Mathematics (with Alfred Tarski, Kazimierz Kuratowski, Wacław Sierpiński and Antoni Zygmund). Numerous mathematicians, scientists, chemists or economists emigrated due to historic vicissitudes, among them Benoit Mandelbrot, Leonid Hurwicz, Alfred Tarski, Joseph Rotblat and Nobel Prize laureates Roald Hoffmann, Georges Charpak and Tadeusz Reichstein.

Demographics
Main articles: Demographics of Poland, List of cities and towns in Poland, Metropolitan areas in Poland, Polish people, and Polish diaspora
Warsaw is the largest city in Poland, and an economic hub of the country.

Poland has a population of approximately 38.2 million as of 2021, and is the ninth-most populous country in Europe, as well as the fifth-most populous member state of the European Union.[317] It has a population density of 122 inhabitants per square kilometre (320 inhabitants/mi2).[318] The total fertility rate was estimated at 1.2 children born to a woman in 2023, which is among the world's lowest.[319] Furthermore, Poland's population is aging significantly, and the country has a median age of 42.2.[320]

Around 60% of the country's population lives in urban areas or major cities and 40% in rural zones.[321] In 2020, 50.2% of Poles resided in detached dwellings and 44.3% in apartments.[322] The most populous administrative province or state is the Masovian Voivodeship and the most populous city is the capital, Warsaw, at 1.8 million inhabitants with a further 2–3 million people living in its metropolitan area.[323][324][325] The metropolitan area of Katowice is the largest urban conurbation with a population between 2.7 million[326] and 5.3 million residents.[327] Population density is higher in the south of Poland and mostly concentrated in Upper Silesia, between the cities of Wrocław and Kraków.[328]

The metropolitan area of Katowice is the largest urban conurbation, with Upper Silesia being the most densely populated region in Poland.

In the 2011 Polish census, 37,310,341 people reported Polish identity, 846,719 Silesian, 232,547 Kashubian and 147,814 German. Other identities were reported by 163,363 people (0.41%) and 521,470 people (1.35%) did not specify any nationality.[329] Official population statistics do not include migrant workers who do not possess a permanent residency permit or Karta Polaka.[330] More than 1.7 million Ukrainian citizens worked legally in Poland in 2017.[331] The number of migrants is rising steadily; the country approved 504,172 work permits for foreigners in 2021 alone.[332]

According to the 2021 census, ethnic Poles comprise 98.84% of the population, including people who declared Polish heritage alone (96.28%) or both Polish and another ethnicity (2.56%) as responders were allowed to select up to two ethnicities. People who declared only non-Polish ethnicities made up 1.13% of the population and people who did not report their ethnicity numbered 0.03%. The province with the highest percentage of ethnic Poles was the Holy Cross Voivodeship (99.70%), and the region with the lowest share of ethnic Poles was the Silesian Voivodeship (95.49%).[333]

Languages
Main articles: Polish language, Languages of Poland, and Bilingual communes in Poland
Dolina Jadwigi—a bilingual Polish-Kashubian road sign with the village name

Polish is the official and predominant spoken language in Poland, and is one of the official languages of the European Union.[335] It is also a second language in parts of neighbouring Lithuania, where it is taught in Polish-minority schools.[336][337] Contemporary Poland is a linguistically homogeneous nation, with 97% of respondents declaring Polish as their mother tongue.[338] There are currently 15 minority languages in Poland,[339] including one recognised regional language, Kashubian, which is spoken by approximately 100,000 people on a daily basis in the northern regions of Kashubia and Pomerania.[340] Poland also recognises secondary administrative languages or auxiliary languages in bilingual municipalities, where bilingual signs and placenames are commonplace.[341] According to the Centre for Public Opinion Research, around 32% of Polish citizens declared knowledge of the English language in 2015.[342]

Religion
Main article: Religion in Poland
John Paul II, born Karol Wojtyła, held the papacy between 1978 and 2005 and was the first Pole to become Pope.

According to the 2021 census, 71.3% of all Polish citizens adhere to the Catholic Church, with 6.9% identifying as having no religion and 20.6% refusing to answer.[4]

Poland is one of the most religious countries in Europe, where Catholicism remains a part of national identity and Polish-born Pope John Paul II is widely revered.[343][344] In 2015, 61.6% of respondents outlined that religion is of high or very high importance.[345] However, church attendance has greatly decreased in recent years; only 28% of Catholics attended mass weekly in 2021, down from around half in 2000.[346] According to The Wall Street Journal, "Of [the] more than 100 countries studied by the Pew Research Center in 2018, Poland was secularising the fastest, as measured by the disparity between the religiosity of young people and their elders."[343]

Freedom of religion in Poland is guaranteed by the Constitution, and Poland's concordat with the Holy See enables the teaching of religion in public schools.[347] Historically, the Polish state maintained a high degree of religious tolerance and provided asylum for refugees fleeing religious persecution in other parts of Europe.[348] Poland hosted Europe's largest Jewish diaspora, and the country was a centre of Ashkenazi Jewish culture and traditional learning until the Holocaust.[349]

Contemporary religious minorities include Eastern Orthodox Church, Protestants, including Lutherans of the Evangelical-Augsburg Church, Pentecostals in the Pentecostal Church in Poland, Adventists in the Seventh-day Adventist Church. Other smaller Christian denominations include Eastern Catholics, Mariavites, Evangelicalism denominations. Other religions include Jehovah's Witnesses, Jews, Muslims (Tatars), and neopagans, some of whom are members of the Native Polish Church.[350]

Health
Main article: Health in Poland

Medical service providers and hospitals in Poland are subordinate to the Ministry of Health; it provides administrative oversight and scrutiny of general medical practice and is obliged to maintain a high standard of hygiene and patient care. Poland has a universal healthcare system based on an all-inclusive insurance system; state subsidised healthcare is available to all citizens covered by the general health insurance programme of the National Health Fund (NFZ). Private medical complexes exist nationwide; over 50% of the population uses both public and private sectors.[351][352][353]

According to the Human Development Report from 2020, the average life expectancy at birth is 79 years (around 75 years for an infant male and 83 years for an infant female);[234] the country has a low infant mortality rate (4 per 1,000 births).[354] In 2019, Poland was the 15th-largest importer of medications and pharmaceutical products.[355] In the same year, the principal cause of death was ischemic heart disease; diseases of the circulatory system accounted for 45% of all deaths.[356] Moreover, the increasing rate of childhood obesity in Poland is one of the fastest in Europe.[357] Health professionals warn that if these rapid upward trajectories continue, the current generation of children could be the first in modern history to have a shorter life expectancy than their parents due to obesity-related complications like type 2 diabetes and hypertension.[358]

Education
Main articles: Education in Poland and Universities in Poland
Jagiellonian University in Kraków, one of the world's oldest institutions of higher learning

The Jagiellonian University founded in 1364 by Casimir III in Kraków was the first institution of higher learning established in Poland, and is one of the oldest universities still in continuous operation.[359] Poland's Commission of National Education (Komisja Edukacji Narodowej), established in 1773, was the world's first state ministry of education.[360][361] In 2018, the Programme for International Student Assessment, coordinated by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, placed Poland's educational output as one of the highest in the OECD, ranking 5th by student attainment and 6th by student performance in 2022.[362][363]

The framework for primary, secondary and higher tertiary education are established by the Ministry of Education and Science. One year of kindergarten is compulsory for six-year-olds.[364][365] Primary education traditionally begins at the age of seven, although children aged six can attend at the request of their parents or guardians.[365] Elementary school spans eight grades and secondary schooling is dependent on student preference – a four-year high school (liceum), a five-year technical school (technikum) or various vocational studies (szkoła branżowa) can be pursued by individual pupils.[365] A liceum or technikum is concluded with a maturity exit exam (matura), which must be passed in order to apply for a university or other institutions of higher learning.[366]

In Poland, there are over 500 university-level institutions,[367] with numerous faculties.[368] The University of Warsaw and Warsaw Polytechnic, the University of Wrocław, Adam Mickiewicz University in Poznań and the University of Technology in Gdańsk are among the most prominent.[369] There are three conventional academic degrees in Poland – licencjat or inżynier (first cycle), magister (second cycle) and doktor (third cycle qualification).[370]

Culture
Main article: Culture of Poland
The Polish White Eagle is Poland's enduring national and cultural symbol.

The culture of Poland is closely connected with its intricate 1,000-year history, and forms an important constituent in the Western civilisation.[371] The Poles take great pride in their national identity which is often associated with the colours white and red, and exuded by the expression biało-czerwoni ("whitereds").[372] National symbols, chiefly the crowned white-tailed eagle, are often visible on clothing, insignia and emblems.[373] The architectural monuments of great importance are protected by the National Heritage Board of Poland.[374] Over 100 of the country's most significant tangible wonders were enlisted onto the Historic Monuments Register,[375] with further 18 being recognised by UNESCO as World Heritage Sites.[376]

Holidays and traditions
See also: Christmas in Poland
All Saints' Day on 1 November is one of the most important public holidays in Poland.

There are 14 government-approved annual public holidays – New Year on 1 January, Three Kings' Day on 6 January, Easter Sunday and Easter Monday, Labour Day on 1 May, Constitution Day on 3 May, Pentecost, Corpus Christi, Feast of the Assumption on 15 August, All Saints' Day on 1 November, Independence Day on 11 November and Christmastide on 24, 25 and 26 December.[377]

Particular traditions and superstitious customs observed in Poland are not found elsewhere in Europe. Though Christmas Eve (Wigilia) had not been a public holiday until 2025,[378] it remains the most memorable day of the entire year. Trees are decorated on 24 December, hay is placed under the tablecloth to resemble Jesus' manger, Christmas wafers (opłatek) are shared between gathered guests and a twelve-dish meatless supper is served that same evening when the first star appears.[379] An empty plate and seat are symbolically left at the table for an unexpected guest.[380] On occasion, carolers journey around smaller towns with a folk Turoń creature until the Lent period.[381]

A widely popular doughnut and sweet pastry feast occurs on Fat Thursday, usually 52 days prior to Easter.[382] Eggs for Holy Sunday are painted and placed in decorated baskets that are previously blessed by clergymen in churches on Easter Saturday. Easter Monday is celebrated with pagan dyngus festivities, where the youth is engaged in water fights.[383][382] Cemeteries and graves of the deceased are annually visited by family members on All Saints' Day; tombstones are cleaned as a sign of respect and candles are lit to honour the dead on an unprecedented scale.[384]

Music and dance
Main article: Music of Poland
Frédéric Chopin was a renowned classical composer and virtuoso pianist.
Artur Rubinstein was one of the greatest concert pianists of the 20th century.

Polish classical music encompasses medieval and early-modern liturgical tradition, regional folk tunes, and a world-renowned piano legacy.[385] Among the leading classical artists were Frédéric Chopin, Artur Rubinstein, Ignacy Jan Paderewski, Krzysztof Penderecki, Henryk Wieniawski, Karol Szymanowski, Witold Lutosławski, and Stanisław Moniuszko. Poland maintains a lively and diverse music scene which recognises its own music and entertainment genres, such as sung poetry and disco polo.[386] Jazz and metal genres are also particularly popular, and the country has become a major venue for large-scale music festivals, chief among which are the Pol'and'Rock Festival, Open'er Festival, Opole Festival and Sopot Festival.[387][388]

The origins of Polish music can be traced to 13th-century polyphonic compositions associated with the Notre Dame School.[389] The anthemic melodies of Bogurodzica and God Is Born may also date back to this period, however, the first notable composer, Nicholas of Radom, lived in the 15th century.[389][390] In the 16th century, Venceslaus Samotulinus and Mikołaj Gomółka gained recognition, and Diomedes Cato, an Italian lutenist at the court of Sigismund III, imported musical styles from southern Europe.[391] At the end of the 18th century, Polish classical music evolved into national forms, and Wojciech Bogusławski is credited for composing the first Polish national opera in 1794.[392] Halka, The Haunted Manor, and King Roger are canons of 19th and early 20th-century Polish opera.[393] The interwar period of 1918–1939 saw the rise of jazz, foxtrot, Polish tango and a strong cabaret culture.[394]

Polish choreography is a sophisticated ethnographic system comprising five national folk dances; the polonaise, mazurka, krakowiak (cracovienne), kujawiak, and oberek as well as various types of polkas.[395] These are performed in national costumes for larger cultural events and accompanied by instruments such as the fiddle, bass, clarinet and accordion across much of Poland, and by the highlander bagpipes in the southern mountainous areas.[396] Since 2023, the polonaise has been inscribed in the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage List.[397] Polish dances also spread across much of the Nordic countries and developed into the polska family of music and dance.[398]

Art
Main articles: Art in Poland and Young Poland
Jan Matejko, leading Polish history painter whose works depict Poland's heritage and key historical events
Lady with an Ermine (1490) by Leonardo da Vinci is displayed in the Czartoryski Museum in Kraków.

Art in Poland has invariably reflected European trends, with Polish painting pivoted on folklore, Catholic themes, historicism and realism, but also on Impressionism and romanticism. An important art movement was Young Poland, developed in the late 19th century for promoting decadence, symbolism and Art Nouveau. Since the 20th century Polish documentary art and photography has enjoyed worldwide fame, especially the Polish School of Posters.[399] One of the most distinguished paintings in Poland is Lady with an Ermine (1490) by Leonardo da Vinci.[400]

Internationally renowned Polish artists include Jan Matejko (historicism), Jacek Malczewski (symbolism), Stanisław Wyspiański (art nouveau), Henryk Siemiradzki (Roman academic art), Tamara de Lempicka (art deco), and Zdzisław Beksiński (dystopian surrealism).[401] Several Polish artists and sculptors were also acclaimed representatives of avant-garde, constructivist, minimalist and contemporary art movements, including Katarzyna Kobro, Władysław Strzemiński, Magdalena Abakanowicz, Alina Szapocznikow, Igor Mitoraj and Wilhelm Sasnal.

Notable art academies in Poland include the Kraków Academy of Fine Arts, Academy of Fine Arts in Warsaw, Art Academy of Szczecin, University of Fine Arts in Poznań and the Geppert Academy of Fine Arts in Wrocław. Contemporary works are exhibited at Zachęta, Ujazdów, and MOCAK art galleries.[402]

Architecture
Main article: Architecture of Poland
St. Mary's Basilica on the Main Market Square in Kraków is an example of Brick Gothic architecture.
The 16th-century City Hall of Poznań illustrates the Renaissance style.

The architecture of Poland reflects European architectural styles, with strong historical influences derived from Italy, Germany, and the Low Countries.[403] Settlements founded on Magdeburg Law evolved around central marketplaces (plac, rynek), encircled by a grid or concentric network of streets forming an old town (stare miasto).[404] Poland's traditional landscape is characterised by ornate churches, city tenements and town halls.[405] Cloth hall markets (sukiennice) were once an abundant feature of Polish urban architecture.[406] The mountainous south is known for its Zakopane chalet style, which originated in Poland.[407]

The earliest architectonic trend was Romanesque (c. 11th century), but its traces in the form of circular rotundas are scarce.[408] The arrival of brick Gothic (c. 13th century) defined Poland's most distinguishable medieval style, exuded by the castles of Malbork, Lidzbark, Gniew and Kwidzyn as well as the cathedrals of Gniezno, Gdańsk, Wrocław, Frombork and Kraków.[409] The Renaissance (16th century) gave rise to Italianate courtyards, defensive palazzos and mausoleums.[410] Decorative attics with pinnacles and arcade loggias are elements of Polish Mannerism, found in Poznań, Lublin and Zamość.[411][412] Foreign artisans often came at the expense of kings or nobles, whose palaces were built thereafter in the Baroque, Neoclassical and Revivalist styles (17th–19th century).[413]

Primary building materials timber and red brick were used extensively in Polish folk architecture,[414] and the concept of a fortified church was commonplace.[415] Secular structures such as dworek manor houses, farmsteads, granaries, mills and country inns are still present in some regions or in open air museums (skansen).[416] However, traditional construction methods faded in the early-mid 20th century due to urbanisation and the construction of functionalist housing estates and residential areas.[417]

Literature
Main articles: Polish literature and History of philosophy in Poland
Adam Mickiewicz, whose national epic poem Pan Tadeusz (1834) is considered a masterpiece of Polish literature
Joseph Conrad, author of popular books such as Heart of Darkness (1899) and Nostromo (1904)

The literary works of Poland have traditionally concentrated around the themes of patriotism, spirituality, social allegories and moral narratives.[418] The earliest examples of Polish literature, written in Latin, date to the 12th century.[419] The first Polish phrase Day ut ia pobrusa, a ti poziwai (officially translated as "Let me, I shall grind, and you take a rest") was documented in the Book of Henryków and reflected the use of a quern-stone.[420] It has been since included in UNESCO's Memory of World Register.[421] The oldest extant manuscripts of fine prose in Old Polish are the Holy Cross Sermons and the Bible of Queen Sophia,[422] and Calendarium cracoviense (1474) is Poland's oldest surviving print.[423]

The poets Jan Kochanowski and Nicholas Rey became the first Renaissance authors to write in Polish.[424] Prime literarians of the period included Dantiscus, Modrevius, Goslicius, Sarbievius and theologian John Laski. In the Baroque era, Jesuit philosophy and local culture greatly influenced the literary techniques of Jan Andrzej Morsztyn (Marinism) and Jan Chryzostom Pasek (sarmatian memoirs).[425] During the Enlightenment, playwright Ignacy Krasicki composed the first Polish-language novel.[426] Poland's leading 19th-century romantic poets were the Three Bards – Juliusz Słowacki, Zygmunt Krasiński and Adam Mickiewicz, whose epic poem Pan Tadeusz (1834) is a national classic.[427] In the 20th century, the English impressionist and early modernist writings of Joseph Conrad made him one of the most eminent novelists of all time.[428][429]

Contemporary Polish literature is versatile, with its fantasy genre having been particularly praised.[430] The philosophical sci-fi novel Solaris by Stanisław Lem and The Witcher series by Andrzej Sapkowski are celebrated works of world fiction.[431] Poland has six Nobel-Prize winning authors – Henryk Sienkiewicz (Quo Vadis; 1905), Władysław Reymont (The Peasants; 1924), Isaac Bashevis Singer (1978), Czesław Miłosz (1980), Wisława Szymborska (1996), and Olga Tokarczuk (2018).[432][433][434]

Cuisine
Main article: Polish cuisine
Kielbasa sausage, a staple of Polish cuisine, with pickled cucumbers and rye bread

The cuisine of Poland is eclectic, with many regional varieties, sharing some similarity with other neighbouring cuisines.[435] Among the staple or regional dishes are pierogi (filled dumplings), kielbasa (sausage), bigos (hunter's stew), kotlet schabowy (breaded cutlet), gołąbki (cabbage rolls), barszcz (borscht), żurek (soured rye soup), oscypek (smoked cheese), and tomato soup.[436][437] Bagels, a type of bread roll, also originated in Poland.[438]

Traditional dishes are hearty and abundant in pork, potatoes, eggs, cream, mushrooms, regional herbs, and sauce.[439] Polish food is characteristic for its various kinds of kluski (soft dumplings), soups, cereals and a variety of breads and open sandwiches. Salads, including mizeria (cucumber salad), coleslaw, sauerkraut, carrot and seared beets, are common. Meals conclude with a dessert such as sernik (cheesecake), makowiec (poppy seed roll), or napoleonka (mille-feuille) cream pie.[440]

Traditional alcoholic beverages include honey mead, widespread since the 13th century, beer, wine and vodka.[441] The world's first written mention of vodka originates from Poland.[442] The most popular alcoholic drinks at present are beer and wine which took over from vodka more popular in the years 1980–1998.[443] Grodziskie, sometimes referred to as "Polish Champagne", is an example of a historical beer style from Poland.[444] Tea remains common in Polish society since the 19th century, whilst coffee is drunk widely since the 18th century.[445]

Fashion and design
Further information: Category:Polish fashion
Traditional polonaise dresses, 1780–1785

Several Polish designers and stylists left a legacy of beauty inventions and cosmetics; including Helena Rubinstein and Maksymilian Faktorowicz, who created a line of cosmetics company in California known as Max Factor and formulated the term "make-up" which is now widely used as an alternative for describing cosmetics.[446] Faktorowicz is also credited with inventing modern eyelash extensions.[447][448] As of 2020, Poland possesses the sixth-largest cosmetic market in Europe. Inglot Cosmetics is the country's largest beauty products manufacturer,[449] and the retail store Reserved is the country's most successful clothing store chain.[450]

Historically, fashion has been an important aspect of Poland's national consciousness or cultural manifestation, beginning with the poulaine pointed footwear in the 14th century, to developing an endemic style known as Sarmatism at the turn of the 17th century.[451] The national dress and etiquette of Poland reached the court at Versailles, where French dresses inspired by Polish garments included robe à la polonaise and the witzchoura. The scope of influence also entailed furniture; rococo Polish beds with canopies became fashionable in châteaus.[452] Sarmatism eventually faded in the wake of the 18th century.[451]

Cinema
Main article: Cinema of Poland
Andrzej Wajda (1926–2016), renowned Polish film director

The cinema of Poland traces its origins to 1894, when inventor Kazimierz Prószyński patented the Pleograph and subsequently the Aeroscope, the first successful hand-held operated film camera.[453][454] In 1897, Jan Szczepanik constructed the Telectroscope, a prototype of television transmitting images and sounds.[453] They are both recognised as pioneers of cinematography.[453] Poland has also produced influential directors, film producers and actors, many of whom were active in Hollywood, chiefly Roman Polański, Andrzej Wajda, Pola Negri, Samuel Goldwyn, the Warner brothers, Max Fleischer, Agnieszka Holland, Krzysztof Zanussi and Krzysztof Kieślowski.[455]

The themes commonly explored in Polish cinema include history, drama, war, culture and black realism (film noir).[453][454] In the 21st-century, two Polish productions won the Academy Awards – The Pianist (2002) by Roman Polański and Ida (2013) by Paweł Pawlikowski.[454] Polish cinematography also created many well-received comedies. The most known of them were made by Stanisław Bareja and Juliusz Machulski.

Media
Main article: Mass media in Poland
Headquarters of the publicly funded national television network TVP in Warsaw

According to the Eurobarometer Report (2015), 78 percent of Poles watch the television daily.[456] In 2020, 79 percent of the population read the news more than once a day, placing it second behind Sweden.[457] Poland has a number of major domestic media outlets, chiefly the public broadcasting corporation TVP, free-to-air channels TVN and Polsat as well as 24-hour news channels TVP Info, TVN 24 and Polsat News.[458] Public television extends its operations to genre-specific programmes such as TVP Sport, TVP Historia, TVP Kultura, TVP Rozrywka, TVP Seriale and TVP Polonia, the latter a state-run channel dedicated to the transmission of Polish-language telecasts for the Polish diaspora. In 2020, the most popular types of newspapers were tabloids and socio-political news dailies.[456]

Poland is a major European hub for video game developers and among the most successful companies are CD Projekt, Techland, The Farm 51, CI Games and People Can Fly.[459] Some of the popular video games developed in Poland include The Witcher trilogy and Cyberpunk 2077.[459] The Polish city of Katowice also hosts Intel Extreme Masters, one of the biggest esports events in the world.[459]

Sports
Main articles: Sport in Poland and Poland at the Olympics
The Kazimierz Górski National Stadium in Warsaw, home of the national football team

Motorcycle speedway, volleyball and association football are among the country's most popular sports, with a rich history of international competitions.[460][461] Track and field, basketball, handball, boxing, MMA, ski jumping, cross-country skiing, ice hockey, tennis, fencing, swimming, and weightlifting are other popular sports. The golden era of football in Poland occurred throughout the 1970s and went on until the early 1980s when the Polish national football team achieved their best results in any FIFA World Cup competitions finishing third place in the 1974 and the 1982 tournaments. The team won a gold medal in football at the 1972 Summer Olympics and two silver medals, in 1976 and in 1992. In 2012, Poland co-hosted the UEFA European Football Championship.[462]

As of September 2024, the Polish men's national volleyball team is ranked as first in the world.[463] The team won a gold medal at the 1976 Summer Olympics and the gold medal at the FIVB World Championship 1974, 2014 and 2018.[464][465] Mariusz Pudzianowski is a highly successful strongman competitor and has won more World's Strongest Man titles than any other competitor in the world, winning the event in 2008 for the fifth time.[466]

Poland has made a distinctive mark in motorcycle speedway racing. The top Ekstraliga division has one of the highest average attendances for any sport in Poland. The national speedway team of Poland is one of the major teams in international speedway. Individually, Poland has three Speedway Grand Prix World Champions, with the most successful being five-time World Champion Bartosz Zmarzlik who won back-to-back championships in 2019 and 2020 as well as 2022, 2023 and 2024. In 2021, Poland finished runners-up in the Speedway of Nations world championship final, held in Manchester, England in 2021.[467]

In the 21st century, the country has seen a growth of popularity of tennis and produced a number of successful tennis players including World No. 1 Iga Świątek, winner of five Grand Slam singles titles; former World No. 2 Agnieszka Radwanska, winner of 20 WTA career singles titles including 2015 WTA Finals; Top 10 ATP player Hubert Hurkacz; former World No. 1 doubles player Łukasz Kubot, winner of two Grand Slam doubles titles and Jan Zieliński, winner of two Grand Slam mixed doubles titles. Poland also won the 2015 Hopman Cup with Agnieszka Radwańska and Jerzy Janowicz representing the country.[468][469]

Poles made significant achievements in mountaineering, in particular, in the Himalayas and the winter ascending of the eight-thousanders (e.g. Jerzy Kukuczka, Krzysztof Wielicki, Wanda Rutkiewicz). Polish mountains are one of the tourist attractions of the country. Hiking, climbing, skiing and mountain biking and attract numerous tourists every year from all over the world.[298] Water sports are the most popular summer recreation activities, with ample locations for fishing, canoeing, kayaking, sailing and windsurfing especially in the northern regions of the country.[470]

The **Saxon Garden** ([Polish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language "Polish language"): _**Ogród Saski**_) is a 15.5–[hectare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hectare "Hectare")[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Garden#cite_note-przewodnik-2) public garden in central (_[Śródmieście](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C5%9Ar%C3%B3dmie%C5%9Bcie,\_Warsaw "Śródmieście, Warsaw")_) [Warsaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warsaw "Warsaw"), Poland, facing [Piłsudski Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pi%C5%82sudski_Square "Piłsudski Square"). It is the oldest public park in the city. Founded in the late 17th century, it was opened to the public in 1727[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Garden#cite_note-przewodnik-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Garden#cite_note-3) as one of the first publicly accessible parks in the world.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Saxon_Garden&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/50/Plan_Ogrodu_Saskiego.JPG/330px-Plan_Ogrodu_Saskiego.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Plan_Ogrodu_Saskiego.JPG)

Plan of the Saxon Garden

The Saxon Garden was originally the site of [Warsaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warsaw "Warsaw")[fortifications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortification "Fortification"), "[Sigismund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigismund_III_Vasa "Sigismund III Vasa")'s [Ramparts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defensive_wall "Defensive wall")", and of a palace built in 1666 for the powerful aristocrat, [Jan Andrzej Morsztyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Andrzej_Morsztyn "Jan Andrzej Morsztyn").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Garden#cite_note-Kieniewicz-4) The garden was extended in the reign of [King Augustus II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus_II_the_Strong "Augustus II the Strong"), who attached it to the "[Saxon Axis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Axis "Saxon Axis")", a line of parks and palaces linking the western outskirts of Warsaw with the [Vistula River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vistula_River "Vistula River").

The park of the adjoining [Saxon Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Palace "Saxon Palace") was opened to the public on 27 May 1727.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Garden#cite_note-5) It became a public park before [Versailles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palace_of_Versailles "Palace of Versailles") (1791), the [Pavlovsk Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pavlovsk_Palace "Pavlovsk Palace"), [Peterhof Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peterhof_Palace "Peterhof Palace") and [Summer Garden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer_Garden "Summer Garden") (1918), [Villa d'Este](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Villa_d'Este "Villa d'Este") (1920), [Kuskovo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuskovo "Kuskovo") (1939), [Stourhead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stourhead "Stourhead") (1946), [Sissinghurst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sissinghurst_Castle_Garden "Sissinghurst Castle Garden") (1967), [Stowe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stowe,_Buckinghamshire "Stowe, Buckinghamshire") (1990), [Vaux-le-Vicomte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaux-le-Vicomte "Vaux-le-Vicomte") (1990s), and most other world-famous parks and gardens.

Initially a [Baroque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baroque "Baroque")[French-style park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_formal_garden "French formal garden"), in the 19th century it was turned into a Romantic [English-style landscape park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_landscape_garden "English landscape garden"). Destroyed during and after the [Warsaw Uprising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warsaw_Uprising "Warsaw Uprising"), it was partly reconstructed after [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II").

## Features

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Saxon_Garden&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Features")]

### 18th century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Saxon_Garden&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 18th century")]

The garden was a typical example of the Baroque extension of formal vistas inspired by the [park of Versailles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gardens_of_Versailles "Gardens of Versailles"). The park starts from the back façade of the palace, flanking a long alley with many sculptures. The central avenue lead directly to the palace, as was usual in French parks of the era.

Following the completion of the Saxon Palace, the surroundings were included in the structure. The [Brühl Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Br%C3%BChl_Palace,_Warsaw "Brühl Palace, Warsaw") and The Blue Palace, as well as the pavilion known as The Great Salon, were all raised or rebuilt during the initial construction of Saxon Establishment during the reign of [Augustus II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus_II_the_Strong "Augustus II the Strong"). A baroque flower garden with pieces of [turf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sod "Sod"), [flower beds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garden "Garden"), hedges and trees was created. These gardens extended the central axis of a symmetrical building façade in rigorously symmetrical axial designs of patterned [parterres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parterre "Parterre"), gravel walks and formally planted [bosquets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bosquet "Bosquet"). The parterres were laid out from 1713 by Joachim Heinrich Schultze and Gothard Paul Thörl from 1735.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Garden#cite_note-sztuka-6)

*   **[Saxon Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Palace "Saxon Palace")**. A vast palace complex according to [Tylman van Gameren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tylman_van_Gameren "Tylman van Gameren")'s design arose here between 1661 and 1664 for [Jan Andrzej Morsztyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Andrzej_Morsztyn "Jan Andrzej Morsztyn").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Garden#cite_note-Kieniewicz-4) In 1669 the palace was rebuilt and enlarged. The main break was enhanced and a two galleries ended with a double-storied pavillons were added to the palace's alcoves. In 1713 the building was purchased by King Augustus II, who started to repurchase surrounding freeholds and demolishing the buildings.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Garden#cite_note-Kieniewicz-4) Reconstruction of the palace establishment and creating of the [Saxon Axis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Axis "Saxon Axis") passed through three distinct stages – from 1713 to the 1720s according to [Carl Friedrich Pöppelmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Frederick_P%C3%B6ppelmann "Carl Frederick Pöppelmann")'s and Joachim Daniel von Jauch's design, secondly to 1733 and completion in 1748 by [Augustus III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus_III_of_Poland "Augustus III of Poland") "the Corpulent".[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Garden#cite_note-Kieniewicz-4) The palace was remodeled in 1842. During [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), the Saxon Palace was [blown up by the Germans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_destruction_of_Warsaw "Planned destruction of Warsaw") after the collapse of the [Warsaw Uprising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warsaw_Uprising "Warsaw Uprising") in 1944.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Garden#cite_note-7)
*   **[Brühl Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Br%C3%BChl_Palace,_Warsaw "Brühl Palace, Warsaw")**, former palace of [Jerzy Ossoliński](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerzy_Ossoli%C5%84ski "Jerzy Ossoliński"), was rebuilt between 1681 and 1697 by Tylman van Gameren.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Garden#cite_note-bruhl-8) Purchased by [Heinrich von Brühl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heinrich_von_Br%C3%BChl "Heinrich von Brühl") in 1750, on his request it was reconstructed by Johann Friedrich Knöbel and Joachim Daniel von Jauch between 1754 and 1759.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Garden#cite_note-Kieniewicz-4) The two outbuildings were built in that time and put together with the palace. Later another two outbuildings were added and weaved together by an enclosure decorated with sculptures. The central limb of the building was enhanced and covered with a [mansard roof](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mansard_roof "Mansard roof"). During 1932–37 the palace was adapted for use as the [Ministry for Foreign Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Foreign_Affairs_of_the_Republic_of_Poland "Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Poland") of the new Polish Republic. It was deliberately destroyed by the Germans on December 18, 1944.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Garden#cite_note-bruhl-8)
*   **Sandstone statues**, a part of the rich collection of sculptures removed to [Saint Petersburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Petersburg "Saint Petersburg") after recapturing the city by [Marshal Suvorov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Suvorov "Alexander Suvorov") in 1794, and placed in the [Summer Garden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer_Garden "Summer Garden").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Garden#cite_note-sztuka-6) According to the 1745 plan of the Saxon Garden there were 70 postuments in the garden, and in 1797 there were only 37 sculptures left;[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Garden#cite_note-sztuka-6) only 20 of them have been preserved until our times. Four of these sculptures were completely destroyed during the blowing up of the Saxon Palace in 1944, but they were later reconstructed.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Garden#cite_note-sztuka-6) Included are groups of sculptures, including [Arithmetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arithmetic "Arithmetic"), [Astronomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronomy "Astronomy"), [Bacchus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dionysus "Dionysus"), [Flora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flora_(mythology) "Flora (mythology)"), [Geography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography "Geography"), two sculptures identified as Glory, Instruct, [Intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intelligence "Intelligence"), [Intellect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intellect "Intellect"), [Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justice "Justice"), [Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicine "Medicine"), Military Architecture, [Painting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Painting "Painting"), [Poetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poetry "Poetry"), [Rationality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rationality "Rationality"), [Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science "Science"), [Sculpture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sculpture "Sculpture"), [Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus_(mythology) "Venus (mythology)") and Winter. They were generally made before 1745 by anonymous Warsaw sculptors under the direction of Johann Georg Plersch.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Garden#cite_note-sztuka-6)
*   **The Great Salon**, situated on the axis in the center of a Saxon Garden, was intended simply to provide a suitable end to the main garden axis. It was constructed after 1720 according to [Matthäus Daniel Pöppelmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matth%C3%A4us_Daniel_P%C3%B6ppelmann "Matthäus Daniel Pöppelmann")'s design.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Garden#cite_note-Kieniewicz-4) The building was opened to the garden by semicircular porte-fenêtres and [oculi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oculus_(architecture) "Oculus (architecture)"). A terrace above the ground level of the building was enclosed by an attic decorated with vases; also, two outhouses from both sides were added. The Great Salon was demolished in 1817.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Garden#cite_note-sztuka-6)
*   **[Operalnia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operalnia "Operalnia")**, the 500-seat opera house,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Garden#cite_note-9) was opened in 1748. It was built under the architect Carl Friedrich Pöppelmann and modelled on the Small Theatre in [Dresden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dresden "Dresden"), built by Christoph Bayer in 1687. The interior was decorated in a heavy, sumptuous baroque style by the court artists. On November 19, 1765, in Operalnia, the actors of The Majesty put on the premiere of [Józef Bielawski's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J%C3%B3zef_Bielawski_(poet)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Józef Bielawski (poet) (page does not exist)")[[pl](https://pl.wikipedia.org/wiki/J%C3%B3zef%20Bielawski%20(poeta) "pl:Józef Bielawski (poeta)"); [de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/J%C3%B3zef%20Bielawski%20(Dichter) "de:Józef Bielawski (Dichter)")]_Intruders_ (_Natręci_), a comedy which was a loose adaptation of a play by [Molière](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moli%C3%A8re "Molière").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Garden#cite_note-Kieniewicz-4) Since the acting team had all the features of a fully professional and national group (they performed in Polish and earned their living through acting), November 19 is the anniversary of the establishment of the [National Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Theatre,_Warsaw "National Theatre, Warsaw"). The National stage belonged to the elements of the educational and cultural reform programme in the falling Republic of Poland, prepared by King [Stanisław August Poniatowski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanis%C5%82aw_August_Poniatowski "Stanisław August Poniatowski"). Over decades this theatre, taking care of the works of Polish playwrights, was the ground on which the cultural development of Polish people thrived. The building was demolished in 1772.
*   **The Blue Palace**. It takes its name from the colour of the roof. the palace was purchased by King Augustus II for his daughter [Anna Karolina Orzelska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna_Karolina_Orzelska "Anna Karolina Orzelska") from bishop [Teodor Andrzej Potocki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teodor_Andrzej_Potocki "Teodor Andrzej Potocki"). The palace was rebuilt in 1726 by [Joachim Daniel von Jauch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joachim_Daniel_von_Jauch "Joachim Daniel von Jauch") and Johann Sigmund Deybel.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Garden#cite_note-Kieniewicz-4) The King wanted to offer it to Anna as a Christmas present. In six weeks, the palace was renovated by 300 masons and craftsmen working night and day.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Garden#cite_note-perelki-10) The courtyard, encompassed by a walled enclosure, had two gates. Column galleries were situated on both sides of the garden façade. A backside garden (integral part of the Saxon Garden) and a cascade fountain were designed by Carl Friedrich Pöppelmann.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Garden#cite_note-Kieniewicz-4) Since 1811, it has been the property of the [Zamoyski family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zamoyski_family "Zamoyski family") which remodeled it in a late [Neoclassical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neoclassical_architecture "Neoclassical architecture") style. The palace was rebuilt after the war devastations.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Garden#cite_note-perelki-10)
*   **The Church of St. Anthony of Padua** and Reformed Franciscan Monastery was founded in 1623 in gratitude for the capture of [Smolensk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smolensk "Smolensk") on June 13, 1611 (Liturgical Feasts of [Saint Anthony of Padua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_of_Padua "Anthony of Padua")) by [Sigismund III Vasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigismund_III_Vasa "Sigismund III Vasa") and dedicated on May 13, 1635. This church was heavily damaged during the [Deluge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deluge_(history) "Deluge (history)") by the [Transylvanian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transylvania "Transylvania") army of [George II Rákóczi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_II_R%C3%A1k%C3%B3czi "George II Rákóczi").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Garden#cite_note-Kieniewicz-4) The new church was founded by Castellan Stanisław Leszczyc-Skarszewski.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Garden#cite_note-anthony-11) Work began in 1668 following the plan of Józef Szymon Bellotti. In 1734, the church became the parish church of the royal court in the Saxon Palace. The king ordered a special loge for him and his wife to be built on the left side of the presbytery (1734–35), and the royal sculptor Johann Georg Plersch created the sculptures inside. The church was partly destroyed during the [Warsaw Uprising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warsaw_Uprising "Warsaw Uprising").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Garden#cite_note-anthony-11)
*   **The Iron Gate** was a part of The Saxon Establishment, which itself had a shape of a pentagon covered an area of around 17 ha. The gate was constructed according to Joachim Daniel von Jauch's design after 1735,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Garden#cite_note-12) together with other buildings of the [Saxon Axis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Axis "Saxon Axis") border, like Mounted Crown Guards barracks, a wall with bastions from the south and west, or the Blue Palace. It was embellished with cartouches with [Polish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coat_of_arms_of_Poland "Coat of arms of Poland") and [Lithuanian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coat_of_arms_of_Lithuania "Coat of arms of Lithuania")[coats of arms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coat_of_arms "Coat of arms"). The gate was demolished in 1821.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Garden#cite_note-sztuka-6)

View of The Saxon Establishment from the north painted by [Bernardo Bellotto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernardo_Bellotto "Bernardo Bellotto")_il Canaletto_ of 1764 shows a main entrance to the palace from Wielopole with The Iron Gate and the 21 m-high garden [gloriette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gloriette "Gloriette"), so-called Great Salon.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Garden#cite_note-Kieniewicz-4)

*   **[Tomb of the Unknown Soldier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomb_of_the_Unknown_Soldier,_Warsaw "Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, Warsaw")**, dedicated to the unknown soldiers who have given their lives for Poland. It is one of many such national tombs of unknowns that were erected after [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I"), as well as the most important national symbols of bravery and heroism. In 1925, architect Stanisław Ostrowski produced a design to be located under the arcades of the Saxon Palace in Warsaw.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Garden#cite_note-13) The triple arch of the Tomb is the only remnant of the Saxon Palace colonnade.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Garden#cite_note-14) Here official delegations place wreaths and pay homage to the killed soldiers. The tomb has a change of guards every hour.
*   **Fountain**, with an elaborately carved plaque resting on a shell form basin supported by a scrolled bracket, is often used by dating couples as their meeting place. It was established in 1855. The fountain is the centrepiece of gardens designed by the 19th-century designer [Henryk Marconi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enrico_Marconi "Enrico Marconi") and also one of the most precious urban symbols of Warsaw.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Garden#cite_note-15)
*   **Marble sundial**, an 1863[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Garden#cite_note-16) horizontal [sundial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sundial "Sundial"), is situated close to the big fountain in the centre of the park. It was established by the significant physicist and meteorologist Antoni Szeliga Magier (1762–1837).
*   **Water Tower**, in the northwest part of the Saxon Garden, is situated by the ornamental lake surrounded by [willows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willow "Willow"). This classicist water tower in the shape of a Roman [monopteros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monopteros "Monopteros") was modelled on the [Temple of Vesta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temple_of_Vesta "Temple of Vesta") in [Tivoli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tivoli,_Italy "Tivoli, Italy").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Garden#cite_note-water-17) It was designed in 1852 by the architect Henryk Marconi.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Garden#cite_note-water-17)
*   **Summer Theatre**, a popular summer variéte theatre, existed between 1870 and 1939. It was under [Stanisław Moniuszko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanis%C5%82aw_Moniuszko "Stanisław Moniuszko")'s "rule" at the [Teatr Wielki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teatr_Wielki,_Warsaw "Teatr Wielki, Warsaw") that the wooden Summer Theatre was built in the Saxon Garden, between the Water Tower building and the Blue Palace by Aleksander Zabierzowski. From then on, summer performances from the Warsaw theatres were shown there every year. At the time, the Summer Theatre could seat an audience of 1,065.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Garden#cite_note-18)[Helena Modjeska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helena_Modjeska "Helena Modjeska")[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Garden#cite_note-letni-19) and [Pola Negri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pola_Negri "Pola Negri")[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Garden#cite_note-20) made several appearance there. The theatre burned in September 1939 following a direct hit by an incendiary bomb[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Garden#cite_note-letni-19) and was never restored.
*   **[Palm House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palm_House "Palm House")**, modeled after [Victorian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorian_era "Victorian era") glass and iron structures in England, was built in 1894.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Garden#cite_note-cieplarnia-21) It was created specifically for the exotic palms being collected and introduced to Europe in the 19th century. The elegant design, with its unobstructed space for the spreading crowns of the tall palms, was a perfect marriage of form and function. The structure was destroyed during the [Warsaw Uprising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warsaw_Uprising "Warsaw Uprising") and [Planned destruction of Warsaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planned_destruction_of_Warsaw "Planned destruction of Warsaw") and was never restored.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Garden#cite_note-cieplarnia-21)
*   The Monument dedicated to [Maria Konopnicka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Konopnicka "Maria Konopnicka"), famous Polish poet and writer mainly for children and youth, was unveiled in 1965.
*   The [Stefan Starzyński Monument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stefan_Starzy%C5%84ski_Monument_(Praga-Po%C5%82udnie) "Stefan Starzyński Monument (Praga-Południe)"), statue of city mayor, and leader of the defence efforcts during the [Siege of Warsaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Warsaw_(1939) "Siege of Warsaw (1939)") in 1939, was added in 1981, and removed in 2008

## Microformat

The HTML markup produced by this template emits an [Geo microformat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geo_(microformat) "Geo (microformat)"), which makes the location's [coordinates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geographic_coordinate_system "Geographic coordinate system") (latitude & longitude) [parsable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parsing "Parsing"), so that they can be, say, looked up on a map. As yet, [the standard for doing this](http://microformats.org/wiki/geo-extension-strawman) for off-world bodies is still under development, but is supported in some microformat parsers (e.g. [Swignition](http://buzzword.org.uk/swignition/)). For more information about the use of [microformats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microformat "Microformat") on Wikipedia, please see [the microformat project](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:UF "Wikipedia:UF").

Geo is usually produced by calling {{[coord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Template:Coord "Template:Coord")}}, and uses HTML classes:

*   body
*   geo
*   latitude
*   longitude

**Please do not rename or remove these classes.**

When giving coordinates, please don't be [overly precise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:WikiProject_Geographical_coordinates#Precision "Wikipedia:WikiProject Geographical coordinates").
